title: Draft Comprehensive Plan
text: October 2026 - DRAFT 2 Heritage and Horizons acknowledgments Planning Consultant Team Salem Town Council Sue Clary, Supervisor Scott Eastman Howard Law Brenda Levey Thomas McMorris Committee Members Sue Clary Tom Clary Julie Collier Edward A. Donoghue Larry Haber with planning & grant support from Michael Hatzel Jon Ketchum Shane Nolan Bob Perry Jim Sheldon Noah Simon Kay Tomasi Beth Ulion Jared West Wyatt Wesner Funding This document was prepared with funding provided by the New York State Department of State Environmental Protection Fund. The Salem NY Plan Contents 01 Foundation Introduction 5 Salem at a Glance 9 02 Vision & Framework Vision & Goals 13 Future Land Use Map 19 03 Recommendations Small Business & Economic Development 23 Arts & Institutions 29 Housing 37 Infrastructure 41 Agriculture, Natural Resources, & Open Space 48 Recreation 52 04 Implementation Turning the Plan into Action 55 05 Appendices Appendix A: Review of Local & Regional Plans Appendix B: Community Profile Appendix C: Public Engagement Summaries • Community Survey Summary • Stakeholder Interview & Focus Group Summary • Public Workshop Summaries • Planning Committee Meeting Summaries Appendix D: Detailed Zoning Framework All appendices are provided as a combined online supplement available on the Town of Salem website. 3 4 Heritage and Horizons • 1.o Introduction 01 FOUNDATION • INTRODUCTION The Salem NY Plan • INTRODUCTION Introduction The Town of Salem Comprehensive Plan provides a roadmap for the next 10 to 20 years, guiding decisions about growth, reinvestment, public facilities, land use, and resource protection. Building on previous planning efforts and extensive community engagement, it establishes a shared vision and a set of goals, recommendations, and actions intended to help strengthen Salem while preserving the qualities residents value most. A Comprehensive Plan serves as the Town’s foundational policy document, guiding local decision-making and future actions by identifying community strengths, addressing challenges, and articulating residents’ collective vision for the future. More than simply a planning document, it provides a framework for managing growth and change in a manner that reflects community values and priorities. The Comprehensive Plan establishes the basis for future land use decisions, zoning updates, infrastructure investments, capital improvements, economic development initiatives, natural resource protection, and community development efforts. This plan embraces the key principles of effective comprehensive planning by taking a comprehensive approach to the many factors that influence community life; maintaining a long-range perspective while remaining flexible to changing conditions; focusing on broad policy direction rather than prescriptive regulations; recognizing the relationship between land use, infrastructure, economic vitality, environmental stewardship, and quality of life; and serving as the Town’s primary policy guide for future decision-making. Through this approach, the Salem Comprehensive Plan charts a path that honors the Town’s rich agricultural heritage, historic hamlets, scenic landscapes, and strong sense of community while preparing for future opportunities and challenges. 5 6 Heritage and Horizons Why Update the Comprehensive Plan? Salem’s previous Comprehensive Plan was adopted in 1997. Since then, the former Village of Salem was dissolved; the Town has completed major planning efforts for Main Street, pedestrian connections, and wastewater; and community needs related to housing, agriculture, infrastructure, climate resilience, recreation, and local services have continued to evolve. This update brings those efforts into a single policy framework and addresses priorities that have become more prominent since 1997, including housing choice and rehabilitation, hamlet reinvestment, agricultural viability, infrastructure capacity, flood resilience, and connections among Salem’s arts, cultural, and recreational assets. The Plan also reflects extensive input gathered through surveys, public workshops, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, and ongoing collaboration with the Comprehensive Plan Committee, ensuring that it represents the shared aspirations of Salem residents. The Community Planning Process Developing the Comprehensive Plan was a collaborative process involving residents, elected officials, farms, community organizations, businesses, and planning professionals.. The planning team paired analysis of existing conditions and previous planning documents with extensive public input collected through surveys, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, community workshops, and regular meetings with the Comprehensive Plan Committee. This combination of technical analysis and local experience was used to identify priorities, test ideas, and refine the recommendations in later chapters. Throughout the planning process, New York State’s Smart Growth Principles served as a guiding framework for evaluating existing conditions, engaging the public, developing the Vision and Goals, and preparing recommendations. This approach emphasizes directing investment toward existing community centers, protecting agricultural and natural resources, supporting housing and economic opportunity, strengthening infrastructure, and improving long-term community resilience. Comprehensive Plan Committee The Town of Salem established a Comprehensive Plan Committee to guide development of the Plan. The Committee included residents, local officials, business representatives, farmers, and other community members who provided guidance throughout the planning process. Committee members served as important liaisons between the planning team and the broader community by reviewing draft materials, identifying priorities, assisting with public engagement, and ensuring that recommendations reflected local values and community goals. Committee meetings were held every two to three months throughout the planning process, were publicized in the local media, on the project website, and e-mail announcements, and were open to the public to attend. Meeting summaries are included in Appendix C. Building on Previous Planning Efforts This Comprehensive Plan builds upon and synthesizes recommendations from previous Town, County, regional, and State planning efforts, including: • Salem Comprehensive Plan (1997) • Washington County Economic Development Strategic Plan (2007) • Salem Main Street Renaissance Plan (2017) • Washington County Agricultural and Farmland Protection Plan (2017) • Washington County Tourism Study (2017) • Washington County Housing Transitions: Needs Assessment and Supportive Housing Action Plan (2019) • Forward Together Economic Resiliency Plan (2021) • Salem Pedestrian Connections Plan (2022) • Rural Workforce Transportation Plan (2023) • Adirondack Gateway Safety Action Plan (2025) • Other applicable local laws, zoning updates, and planning initiatives completed since adoption of the previous Comprehensive Plan Together, these efforts provide an important foundation for this Comprehensive Plan while ensuring that recommendations remain coordinated with broader regional initiatives. The Salem NY Plan Planning Framework: Smart Growth Principles The Salem Comprehensive Plan was prepared with funding assistance from the New York State Department of State through the Environmental Protection Fund Smart Growth Comprehensive Planning Program. The planning process incorporated New York State’s Smart Growth Public Infrastructure Policy Act and Smart Growth Principles to guide development of the plan. Smart Growth is a planning approach that seeks to balance economic development, environmental stewardship, infrastructure investment, and community character while creating resilient communities that meet the needs of current and future generations. Rather than promoting growth for its own sake, Smart Growth encourages communities to build upon their existing assets, make efficient use of infrastructure, protect natural resources, and direct investment in ways that strengthen quality of life. For Salem, these principles reinforce many of the priorities identified by residents throughout this planning process, including preserving agricultural lands and scenic landscapes, supporting downtown revitalization, expanding housing opportunities, improving infrastructure, protecting natural resources, and maintaining the rural character that defines the community. New York State Smart Growth Principles This Comprehensive Plan was developed consistent with the following Smart Growth Principles established by New York State: 1. Allow for and encourage neighborhoods with a mix of uses, such as residential, commercial and community spaces. 2. Enable a diverse mix of housing types, providing opportunity and choice for people of all ages, abilities and incomes. 3. Prioritize infill and redevelopment of existing buildings to revitalize neighborhoods and downtowns, including areas around public transit. 4. Provide well-planned, equitable, and accessible public spaces for people of all ages and abilities. 5. Encourage compact neighborhood design and concentrated development around existing infrastructure. 6. Preserve open space, agricultural resources and natural resources. Land preservation directs development toward areas that are already developed, minimizing encroachment on open space and natural resources. 7. Prioritize transportation options that are safe and accessible for everyone, including pedestrians, cyclists and public transit users. 8. Promote climate resiliency and adaptation, preferably through nature-based solutions, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. 9. Build on unique traits to create an attractive and welcoming community with a strong sense of place. Each community has unique attributes, such as historic buildings, natural surroundings, local traditions, or small businesses. 10. Engage in an inclusive, collaborative public planning process that considers the needs and character of the community. Throughout this Comprehensive Plan, these principles are reflected in the vision, goals, recommendations, and implementation strategy. Collectively, they provide a framework for guiding future land use decisions, infrastructure investments, economic development initiatives, environmental stewardship, and community improvements in a manner that is consistent with Salem’s values and long-term aspirations. 7 Heritage and Horizons 8 Public Participation Community engagement was central to development of the Salem Comprehensive Plan. The Town employed a variety of outreach methods designed to ensure that residents, businesses, property owners, farmers, seasonal residents, and other stakeholders had multiple opportunities to participate throughout the planning process. These efforts generated valuable feedback that helped shape the community vision, goals, and recommendations. Public participation activities included: • Community Survey: An online and printed survey collected community input regarding priorities, challenges, opportunities, and future goals across a range of planning topics. • Stakeholder Interviews and Focus Groups: Interviews and focus group discussions were conducted with Town officials, community organizations, businesses, agricultural representatives, emergency service providers, educators, and other stakeholders to better understand local issues and opportunities. • Community Workshops: Public workshops invited residents to discuss community strengths, challenges, future vision, and draft recommendations. • Public Hearings: Public hearings before the Comprehensive Plan Committee and Town Board provided formal opportunities for residents to review and comment on the draft Comprehensive Plan prior to adoption. These activities were promoted through the project website, social media, local media outlets, email announcements, flyers, and other community outreach efforts. Summaries of public engagement activities and comments received throughout the planning process are included in Appendix C. The Salem NY Plan • INTRODUCTION Salem at a Glance Salem is a rural community shaped by working farms, historic hamlets, waterways and open lands, a strong arts and cultural community, and a long tradition of civic involvement. Located in eastern Washington County along the Vermont border, the Town has maintained a relatively stable population. That stability has helped preserve Salem’s while landscape and settlement pattern, but it also means that an aging housing stock, limited infrastructure, changing demographics, and the need to sustain local institutions and businesses are especially important to the Town’s future. The Community Profile and public engagement process point to a consistent set strengths to build upon and emerging challenges that warrant proactive planning. Agriculture remains one of Salem’s defining assets and continues to shape both its economy and landscape. Nearly three-quarters of the Town lies within New York State Certified Agricultural Districts, approximately one-third of the Town’s land area is actively used for agriculture, and Salem contains roughly one-fifth of all farms in Washington County. Working farms, open fields, forests, and scenic rural vistas contribute not only to the local economy, but also to the community character residents consistently identified as one of Salem’s greatest strengths. Protecting farmland, supporting farm viability, and minimizing conflicts between agricultural and non-agricultural land uses emerged as recurring themes throughout the planning process. 9 10 Heritage and Horizons The Town’s development pattern reflects its agricultural heritage. Most new development has occurred as dispersed rural residential growth along existing roadways, while the former Village of Salem and the Hamlet of Shushan remain the community’s historic population and service centers. These compact areas contain a mix of housing, businesses, civic uses, and community facilities that distinguish them from the surrounding countryside and make them the most appropriate locations for future reinvestment and growth. Existing infrastructure, walkable street networks, and concentrations of services provide opportunities to accommodate additional housing, support small businesses, encourage adaptive reuse of existing buildings, and strengthen downtown vitality while limiting pressure for scattered development in agricultural and environmentally sensitive areas. Housing emerged as one of Salem’s most significant longterm planning issues. More than half of the Town’s housing was constructed before 1940, new residential construction has been limited, and available choices are dominated by detached single-family homes. Residents identified needs for smaller homes, senior housing, accessory dwelling units, quality rental options, and attainable housing for families and workers. At the same time, rehabilitation costs, property condition, and limited wastewater capacity can make it difficult to reuse older buildings or add housing in the Salem Hamlet. New tools, including the Washington County Land Bank, create additional opportunities to address vacant, deteriorated, and underutilized properties while expanding the range of housing choices. Salem’s population has remained relatively stable over the long term but declined modestly between 2010 and 2020. The Town also has an older population profile and a substantial number of households with limited financial flexibility. These conditions are closely tied to the future of Salem Washington Academy, local businesses, volunteer organizations, and community services: attracting and retaining families helps sustain school enrollment and the local workforce, while housing, transportation, health, and social-service options influence whether older residents can remain in the community. Salem’s proximity to employment centers in Washington County, the Capital Region, and Vermont creates opportunities, but many residents must travel outside the Town for work and services. The Salem NY Plan Natural resources are equally central to Salem’s future. The Battenkill, White Creek, Beaver Brook, other streams, forests, wetlands, floodplains, productive agricultural soils, and scenic landscapes provide ecological, recreational, and economic value while contributing to the Town’s identity and quality of life. Updated FEMA flood mapping and the Town’s history of flooding reinforce the need to consider floodplain function, drainage, stream corridors, and climate resilience in land use and infrastructure decisions. Protecting these systems can reduce risk while supporting agriculture, recreation, tourism, water quality, and public health. Salem’s arts and cultural institutions are unusually prominent for a community of its size. Salem Art Works, the Historic Salem Courthouse, the Georgi Museum, the Shushan Covered Bridge Museum, Bancroft Public Library, local artists, and community events contribute to local identity, tourism, education, and year-round community life. These institutions also create opportunities for stronger coordination, shared programming, placemaking, and creative-economy development. Public engagement repeatedly described the combination of agriculture, arts, history, and neighbors helping neighbors as one of Salem’s most distinctive strengths. Infrastructure is a recurring constraint, as well as an opportunity. The Salem Hamlet has public water but no municipal wastewater system, and previous engineering studies conducted by the Town documented how small lots, aging or undersized septic systems, and water-use restrictions can constrain restaurants, other businesses, building reuse, and new housing. Cellular service gaps, aging electrical infrastructure and limited three-phase capacity, sidewalk gaps, rural transportation needs, 11 and flood-prone roads also affect households, farms, businesses, and emergency services. Addressing these constraints in coordination with land use and development priorities is central to the recommendations that follow. Taken together, these conditions point toward a strategy of reinvesting in Salem’s existing hamlets and institutions while sustaining the working landscape around them. The Plan emphasizes practical improvements that expand housing and economic opportunity, support agriculture and community services, strengthen infrastructure and resilience, and preserve the rural character residents value. A full Community Profile covering these and other topics in detail is included in Appendix B. 12 Heritage and Horizons • 1.o Introduction 02 Vision & FRAMEWORK • INTRODUCTION • INTRODUCTION Vision & Goals This chapter establishes the community’s aspirations for the next ten to twenty years. The vision, principles, and goals were developed through the community survey, stakeholder interviews, focus groups, and the first public workshop, then refined by the Committee. 14 Heritage and Horizons Vision A vision statement is the heart of a Comprehensive Plan. It expresses what Salem aspires to be, not just what it wants to do, but what kind of place it wants to remain and become over the next decade and beyond. This vision emerged directly from the voices of Salem residents, property owners, business owners, and community members who participated in surveys, public workshops, focus groups, and planning committee discussions throughout the planning process. The vision statement serves as the foundation for everything that follows in this plan. The goals, recommendations, and actions in later sections are designed to advance this vision. When future decisions arise, about land use, infrastructure investment, community programs, or zoning, this statement provides a shared reference point to evaluate whether a proposed direction is consistent with what Salem residents said they want. At the same time, update local standards for energyrelated development. Solar and battery energy storage regulations should address siting, setbacks, screening, emergency response, decommissioning, financial assurance, and … while protecting Salem's natural resources and rural character. New Cases: CASE #1560 for Zachary Bischoping of 1098 Quaker Rd, East Aurora, for construction of a post-framed barn in the rear of the property. CASE #1561 for John Keem for 1140 Sweet Rd, East Aurora for construction of a covered front porch. CASE #1562 for Mandy Carl for 2044 and 2052 Lewis Rd, South Wales for combining the two lots. CASE #1563 for Corinthian Homes LLC for 770 West Falls Rd, West Falls, for the construction of a sugar shack on the property. II. Adjourned Cases: none III. Cases for review: none IV. Deliberation and decisions for Cases heard The petitioner or an Authorized Representative must accompany every presentation Please call the Town Clerk’s office at 716-652-3280, or email townclerk@townofaurora.com if you cannot be present at the meeting. The ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS meeting will be held in the Aurora Municipal Center 2nd floor meeting room at 575 Oakwood Ave, East Aurora, NY. Please park in the rear parking lot and enter through the entrance at the rear of the building. There are signs directing you to the second floor via elevator or staircase.

text: The Town of East Greenbush 225 Columbia Turnpike, Rensselaer, New York 12144 TOWN BOARD AGENDA PRE-BOARD MEETING November 10, 2026 Call to Order Pledge of Allegiance Town Board Meeting: 6:00 PM Members of Town Board Present Absent Supervisor J. Conway Councilor H. Kennedy Councilor R. Matters Councilor J. McHugh Councilor L. Koenig The resolutions below are provided to the Town Board in advance of the Official Town Board Meeting to allow time for review and research. The purpose of the Pre-Board Meeting is for the Town Board to publicly discuss resolutions and ask any questions, so they may receive information needed to make an informed decision at the Town Board Meeting. Presentation: Schedule of Meeting: 231-2026 A Resolution to Approve Special Meeting Minutes WHEREAS, the minutes of Town Board meetings, as provided in §106 of Article 7 of the New York Public Officers Law, shall be approved by the Board prior to them being finalized, deemed official and disseminated to the public by the Town Clerk; and WHEREAS, that the minutes of the Town’s Special Meeting held on October 1, 2026 have been presented; and WHEREAS, the Town Board has reviewed these minutes and any necessary corrections have been made; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the minutes of the Town’s Special Meeting held on October 1, 2026 are hereby approved as submitted. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor McHugh and seconded by Councilor Koenig and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: 1 232-2026 A Resolution to Approve the Public Hearing Meeting Minutes WHEREAS, the minutes of Town Board meetings, as provided in §106 of Article 7 of the New York Public Officers Law, shall be approved by the Board prior to them being finalized, deemed official and disseminated to the public by the Town Clerk; and WHEREAS, that the minutes of the Town’s Public Hearing Meeting held on October 14, 2026 have been presented; and WHEREAS, the Town Board has reviewed these minutes and any necessary corrections have been made; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the minutes of the Town’s Public Hearing Meeting held on October 14, 2026 are hereby approved as submitted. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor McHugh and seconded by Councilor Koenig and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: 233-2026 A Resolution Recognizing November as “Men’s Health Awareness Month” WHEREAS, “Movember” is an annual campaign that runs throughout the month of November involving the growing of mustaches to "change the face" of men’s health and raise awareness of men’s health issues, such as prostate cancer, testicular cancer, mental health issues, and suicide prevention; and WHEREAS, significant numbers of male-related health problems could be detected and treated if men’s awareness of these problems was more pervasive. By encouraging men to get involved, Movember aims to increase early cancer detection, diagnosis, effective treatments, and ultimately reduce the number of preventable deaths; and WHEREAS, men who are educated about the value that preventive health can play in prolonging their lifespan and their role as productive family members will be more likely to participate in health screenings; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the Town of East Greenbush wishes to support Men’s Health Awareness Month by raising awareness of the dangers of men’s health issues; and be it further RESOLVED, that the Town Board declares November to be Men’s Health Awareness Month in the Town of East Greenbush. This resolution was duly moved by Councilor McHugh and seconded by Supervisor Conway and brought to a vote as follows: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: 2 234-2026 A Resolution to Authorize a Public Auction of Surplus Equipment WHEREAS, the Town Board of the Town of East Greenbush, County of Rensselaer, State of New York has received a request from the Chief of Police to declare the following equipment as surplus; and WHEREAS, said equipment includes Obsolete Radio Equipment: WHEREAS, the amortization rate of said equipment has far exceeded its life span and is obsolete and is not suited for other departments in Town; and WHEREAS, the Director of Finance has certified that there is no adverse impact to the Town finances; now therefore, be it RESOLVED that the equipment listed is hereby declared as surplus; and be it further RESOLVED that the Purchasing Agent is authorized to dispose of said surplus equipment now owned by and in the custody of the East Greenbush Police Department to Algonquin Communications in exchange for services provided including inventory and memory wiping of all radios. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor McHugh and seconded by Councilor Koenig and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: 235-2026 A Resolution Amending Resolution 245-2025 WHEREAS, the Town Board approved Resolution 245-2025 – approving Troy Industrial to do necessary repairs at the Transfer Station to the Trash Compactor in the amount of $23,722.17; and WHEREAS, the amount that was stated in the resolution inadvertently missed the Freight Charge of $995 which needs to be updated; and WHEREAS, Resolution 245-2025 should be updated to include the following amounts: Field Service Repair Work: $23,722.17 Freight Charge: $995.00 Total Cost: $24,717.17 ; and WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms that this cost can be covered by the 2026 Budget for the Transfer Station 01.8160.4; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the Town Board does hereby approve the amendment of Resolution 245-2025 to include the Freight Charge at $995.00 for a total cost of $24,717.17. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Supervisor Conway and seconded by Councilor Kennedy and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: 3 236-2026 A Resolution Accepting the Resignation of Trevor Cavagnaro as Auto Mechanic in the Highway Department WHEREAS, Trevor Cavagnaro began his position as Auto Mechanic with the East Greenbush Department of Public Works Highway Department in January 2026 and has provided knowledge and skills that are essential to the daily operations of the Mechanics of DPW; and WHEREAS, on Friday, October 30th, 2026, Trevor submitted his resignation to the Commissioner of Public Works, effective Friday, November 13, 2026; and WHEREAS, the office of Public Works Administration would like to thank Trevor for his time and dedication to his position as Auto Mechanic – acknowledging that we would never hold anyone back from bettering themselves and their true potential, we wish Trevor luck in his future endeavors; and WHEREAS, Trevor leaves his position in good standing; and WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms that this resolution will not have an impact on the Town’s Finances, now therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the Town Board does hereby accept the resignation of Trevor Cavagnaro as Auto Mechanic with the Department of Public Works. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor Koenig and seconded by Supervisor Conway and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: 237-2026 A Resolution Authorizing Additional Slip Lining at 9 Park Drive WHEREAS, the Commissioner of Public Works has identified a section of pipe that requires slip lining to address concerns; and WHEREAS, the Department of Public Works has utilized the Storm Sewer slip lining budget allocation and is requesting as an additional $15,387.50 to slip line 125 Linear Feet of 12 inch pipe; and WHEREAS, the problem with this section was identified during a recent water break when the volume of water going through the storm sewer system from Point View Drive caused water to start to back up at 9 Park Drive – a residence that has experienced severe flooding issues during high volume rain events and it is our hope that this can help reduce the flooding events while we continue to work on the storm sewer system and potential long term fixes; and WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms that the use of Sewer fund balance in the amount $15,387.50 to 07.8140.4 Storm Sewer CE to allow for the slip lining at 9 Park Drive; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the Town Board doe hereby approve the use of fund balance to transfer $15,387.50 to 07.8140.4 Storm Sewer CE to allow for 9 Park Drive slip lining of 12” pipe at 125 Linear Feet. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor Matters and seconded by Councilor McHugh and brought to a vote resulting as follows: 4 Councilor R. Matters Councilor J. McHugh Supervisor J. Conway Councilor H. Kennedy Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: VOTED: VOTED: VOTED: VOTED: 238-2026 A Resolution Authorizing the Additional Funding for Construction Inspection for the Railroad Ave Sewer Line Extension Project WHEREAS, the Town Board approved a task order with H.V. LaBarba via Resolution 237-2025 for an amount of $18,000.00; and WHEREAS, H.V. LaBarba contacted the Commissioner of Public Works to address a concern that the original estimate for work included 100 hrs for 2 ½ weeks of anticipated construction of new sanitary sewer on Railroad Ave by American Evergreen at an estimated cost of $18,000. Due to deliberate contractor efforts and the presence of subsoil rock the length of construction time extended the onsite inspection hours by an additional 90 hours, thus incurring an additional fee of $13,500; WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms the use of Sewer Fund Balance will be necessary to cover the overage in the amount of $13,500; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the Town Board does hereby approve the use of Sewer Fund Balance in the amount of $13,500 to 07.8120.4 Sanitary Sewer to cover the additional cost of construction inspection by HV Labarba. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor Kennedy and seconded by Councilor Matters and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: 239-2026 A Resolution Authorizing the Rock Contingency for the Railroad Ave Sewer Main Extension Project WHEREAS, the Town Board authorized the contract with American Evergreen for the Railroad Ave Sewer Main Extension project for a construction amount of $142,000 in Resolution 100-2026; and WHEREAS, the bid and resolution identified the cost of rock removal should the contractor encounter rock while digging at the amount of $200 per cubic yard; and WHEREAS, a contingency amount was not built into the total price, outside of identifying the rock removal at $200/cy; and WHEREAS, American Evergreen has submitted a final payment request that includes 82 cubic yards of rock at a total of $16,400 in addition to the $142,000.00 for a project total of $158,400.00; and WHEREAS, Town Designated Engineer on this project, H.V. LaBarba, has confirmed that this amount of rock was removed and the cause of some delay on the project and has signed off on the contingency amount, recommending the Commissioner to pay the amount; and 5 WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms the use of Sewer Fund Balance will be necessary to cover the overage in the amount of $16,400; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the Town Board does hereby authorize the rock contingency payment in the amount of $16,400 to American Evergreen bringing the project total to $158,400. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor McHugh and seconded by Councilor Koenig and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: 240-2026 A Resolution Accepting the Insurance Recovery and Allocating the Funds to Repair of Damage to the Morgan Road Guiderail WHEREAS, On June 26, 2026 an incident occurred on Morgan Road that resulted in the damage to the Guiderail; and WHEREAS, the incident information, pictures and repair quote were submitted to the Town’s Insurance Company resulting in the Town receiving an Insurance Recovery check in the amount of $13,998.00 for the cost of repair; and WHEREAS, the Commissioner of Public Works is requesting the Insurance Recovery check be transferred to the General Repairs line for Guiderail repairs to allow the repairs to be completed; and WHEREAS, the Town uses Town & Country Bridge and Rail (TCBR) for all guiderail repairs and installation under Rensselaer County Contract (RFB 26-07: Guide Railing Installation); and WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms that the Insurance Recovery check has been deposited into 2.2680 -Insurance Recovery- and a budget amendment is needed to account 02.5110.4-General Repairs- in the amount $13,998 pay for the repair of the guiderail; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the Town Board does hereby accept the Insurance Recovery and authorizes the budget amendment to 02.5110.4 – General Repairs to cover the cost of repair; and be it further, RESOLVED, that the Town Board hereby approves the Commissioner to schedule the guiderail repair on Morgan Road. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor Koenig and seconded by Supervisor Conway and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: 6 241-2026 A Resolution to Set the Transfer Station Rates for 2027 WHEREAS, it is required to establish policies and rates for the use of the East Greenbush Transfer Station on an annual basis; and WHEREAS, the Commissioner of Public Works, Deputy Commissioner of Public Works and Transfer Station personnel met and discussed various fees during the review along with increase in costs charged to the Town by the City of Albany for Landfill Tip Fees, as well as other disposal fees; and WHEREAS, the City of Albany Landfill is facing critical infrastructure issues that could pose a threat to the current processes that the Town of East Greenbush is accustomed to and as a result, we will be meeting with officials in the Capital Region Solid Waste Management Planning Unit (aka Capital Region Recycling Partnership or CRRP) to remain up to date on the plans and processes that will be effective by 2028; and WHEREAS, the annual cost of a Transfer Station permit and punch cards will have a slight increase in 2027; and WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms that this resolution supports the FYE 2027 Budget; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that the proposed policies and rates for 2027 be made effective for the year 2027. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Councilor Kennedy and seconded by Councilor Koenig and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: 242-2026 A Resolution Approving the Adoption of the Annual Budget for Fiscal Year 2027 WHEREAS, pursuant to New York Town Law § 106, subd. 2, the East Greenbush Town Supervisor duly filed a Tentative Budget and budget message in the Office of the Town Clerk on September 30, 2026 (referred to hereinafter as the “Tentative Budget”); and WHEREAS, the Tentative Budget provided for a 1.97% increase in the Town’s Real Property Tax Levy for fiscal year 2027; and WHEREAS, pursuant to New York Town Law § 106, subd. 4, the East Greenbush Town Board, at the scheduled Town Board meeting held on October 28, 2026 duly approved a Preliminary Budget which was filed in the office of the Town Clerk on October 27, 2026 (referred to hereinafter as the “Preliminary Budget”); and WHEREAS, pursuant to New York Town Law § 108, the East Greenbush Town Board duly conducted a public hearing on November 5, 2026 on the Preliminary Budget; and WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms that this resolution will not have a material impact on the Town’s finances because appropriations are matched to revenue and fund balance; and WHEREAS, the final Adopted Budget will have the attachments of the Analysis of Fund Balance Page and Assessor’s Exemption Report; 7 now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that, pursuant to New York Town Law § 109, subd. 1, the Preliminary Budget be, and the same hereby is, duly adopted as the Annual Budget for fiscal year 2027 (referred to hereinafter as the “Adopted Budget”); and be it further RESOLVED, that the Town Clerk shall cause a copy of the Adopted Budget to be duly filed in her office, forthwith, following receipt thereof from the Director of Finance; and be it further RESOLVED, that, pursuant to New York Town Law § 109, subd. 3, the Supervisor, Director of Finance, Comptroller, Receiver of Taxes, and Assessor take all respective action required and/or appropriate relative to the implementation of the Adopted Budget. The foregoing resolution was duly moved by Supervisor Conway and seconded by Councilor Kennedy and brought to a vote resulting as follows: Supervisor J. Conway VOTED: Councilor H. Kennedy VOTED: Councilor R. Matters VOTED: Councilor J. McHugh VOTED: Councilor L. Koenig VOTED: 243-2026 A Resolution to Set the Capital Costs and Operation and Maintenance Costs for the Consolidated General Water District and Consolidated General Sewer District in 2027 WHEREAS, the Town Board wishes to ensure the fiscal stability of the Consolidated General Water District and Consolidated General Sewer District in 2027 and beyond; and WHEREAS, funding for the Consolidated General Water and Consolidated General Sewer District must cover capital costs as well as operation and maintenance costs; and WHEREAS, capital costs will be covered by the cost per unit of assessment charged on the annual tax bill and operation and maintenance costs will be funded by user rates; and WHEREAS, a public hearing was held on the 2027 water and sewer rates on November 5, 2026 and all comments were heard; and WHEREAS, the Director of Finance confirms that this resolution will not have a material impact on the Town’s finances; now, therefore, be it RESOLVED, that payment of capital costs for the Town of East Greenbush Consolidated General Water District and Consolidated General Sewer District for the year January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2027 shall be based upon a Unit of Assessment as set forth in Schedule A, attached hereto and made a part hereof; Motion Second TOWN OF GENEVA, NEW YORK RESOLUTION OF THE TOWN BOARD RESOLUTION NO. 78-2026 Whereas a bond resolution of the Town of Geneva for improvements to Water District 2 was adopted by the Town Board on March 9, 1999, which resulted in a Bond Anticipation Note last renewed with Wayne Bank on or about December 2, 2025, in the amount of $19,731.00, coming due December 2, 2026, together with interest at the rate of 4.39%, and Whereas the full amount due cannot be paid without significant cost to property owners, and it need not be paid in full and may be and has been renewed annually with a payment against principal and the interest due, now therefore, it is RESOLVED the Supervisor of the Town is authorized to pay $3,700.00 toward principal, and the interest due, on or about December 2, 2026, and to sign a new Bond Anticipation Note for a year with Wayne Bank binding the Town of Geneva for the balance due of $16,031.00, plus interest. 14, RESOLUTION NO. 79-2026 — Authorizing a Contract with a Utility Rate Consultant. Motion Second TOWN OF GENEVA, NEW YORK RESOLUTION OF THE TOWN BOARD RESOLUTION NO. 79-2026 Whereas the City of Geneva had a study done of the rates for water and sewer it charges outside users like the Town of Geneva; and Whereas the study proposes a substantial increase in the amount the Town would pay for having wastewater from the Town flow to and be treated at the City’s wastewater treatment plant; and Whereas it is in the best interest of the Town to have an expert in this field review the City’s study and advise the Town regarding the validity of the methodology and conclusions of the City’s study; and 3 | } | i | i Whereas the Town has submitted a Request for Proposals to several companies with the proper expertise, with proposals due by November 9, 2026; now therefore, it is RESOLVED the Town Supervisor and Town Board Member Mitchell Wilber are authorized to select the consultant to assist the Town from those submitting proposals, and the Supervisor is authorized to sign a contract with the selected consultant at an amount not to exceed $25,000.00. 14. Supervisor’s Report: Site work for the Rolling Hill housing project is proceeding, and the sidewalk on Carter Road that was required as part of the project is essentially complete other than final grading and seeding and installing crosswalks in four places. The US Treasury Department has confirmed the Town’s census tract that covers the north part of the Town is an Opportunity Zone, which provides incentives for investors to back development projects there. Community Economic Development Coordinator Jackie Augustine recently attended a conference on how to maximize this opportunity and wilt be working with the Town’s Economic Development Committee to position the Town for growth in this area. The City of Geneva has received the contract from the US Environmental Protection Agency for a grant to enhance responsible materials management for the greater Geneva community. The Town of Genevais a sub-recipient for the three-year grant that began September 30, 2026 and will provide $80,000 to the Town in the first year, $90,000 in the second year and $110,000 in the third year. The Town’s money will support two attendants at the Town’s Recycling and Disposal Station and the City’s Resource Recovery Park on Doran Avenue. Both stations will be open to Town and City residents with a trash card and recycling sticker. The grant will also cover hauling charges, additional signage and education efforts, and equipment to increase the diversion of materials from trash and move City and Town residents to more sustainable living. The grant also supports the creation and expansion of a Reuse Center operated by Reuse Systems, which the Town has been supporting since its launch. Motion to Adjourn The Town Board of the Town of Moreau held a 2026 Budget Workshop at 7:00 p.m. on October 14, 2026 at the Moreau Municipal Building, 351 Reynolds Road, Moreau, Saratoga County, New York. PRESENT: John Donohue Councilmember Laura Garrant Councilmember Patrick Killian Councilmember Mark Stewart Councilmember Jesse A. Fish, Jr. Supervisor ALSO PRESENT: Krystal Smith Bookkeeper Erin Trombley Town Clerk Josh Westfall Town Historian Elizabeth Bennett Confidential Secretary OTHERS PRESENT: Moreau Emergency Squad: Steven VanGuilder; Billie-Jo Krug; Andre Delvaux; Ronald Quinn, Jr.; Michael Beshara TOWN CLERK Appropriations The Town Clerk discussion began with a breakdown of salaries across three of the accounts that fall within the Town Clerk Office prevue: A1330 (Tax Collection), A1410 (Town Clerk), and A6989 (Records Management). Other accounts under the Town Clerk umbrella are B4020 (Registrar of Vital Statistics), and A4068 (Insect Control). Town Clerk Trombley summarized that in the 2026 budget she had distributed both funds and salaries to the three main areas of work proportionally to the amount of time spent on the related tasks, so that was not a change for 2027. Ms. Smith said a 4% raise was proposed across the board. Ms. Trombley asked whether Deputy Clerk 2, Maria Jennings, would receive an additional sum for years of service, a topic discussed in prior meetings. Councilmember Stewart stated that the base Clerk salary in all departments was last set at $48,204. It was explained that all current Clerks will receive a 4% raise to a salary of $50,132 and going forward, new Clerks will be paid $48,204; those who are already on staff will get an annual raise, thereby creating a type of retention incentive. The longer a clerk stays in the position, the more raises they will have accumulated above the starting clerk salary. Under A4068, Insect Control, which covers the expense of providing mosquito dunks for residents. $150 was budgeted for 2027, a reduction of $100 from 2026. Ms. Trombley said there were some leftover from 2026 so there may not be a need to order as many in 2027. Councilmember Stewart questioned whether the proposed amount under A1330.4 (Contractual) would be enough based on past year’s figures. Ms. Trombley said she believed some figures were trimmed based on year- to-date figures, and said some budgeted money in 2026 was not spent on training, for example, due to the departure of former Deputy Clerk 1, Dianne Lewis in the spring. She expressed some concern about having sufficient funds particularly for postage, since there will be more bills mailed, and the postal rate is climbing. Councilmember Stewart asked if staff would attend annual conference in 2027, to which Ms. Trombley responded that likely only one person would be able to attend because the NYSTCA Conference would be held in Niagara Falls in 2027. Bookkeeper Smith asked Ms. Trombley if she wanted an increase. Ms. Trombley deferred to Ms. Smith, not knowing how much of a shortage there might be. Under account A6989, Records Management, Ms. Trombley mentioned the General Code/eCode360 Recodification amount of $12,995 under the .4 (Contractual) line, which was the same as 2026. She said recodification is meant to be done every 10 years or so, and it had been about 25 years since the last one. She explained that the process is for the entire code to be reviewed for continuity within the Town code, as well as 288 The Town Board of the Town of Moreau held a 2026 Budget Workshop at 7:00 p.m. on October 14, 2026 at the Moreau Municipal Building, 351 Reynolds Road, Moreau, Saratoga County, New York. conflicts with State and/or Federal law which may have changed over time. The company recommended timing recodification to coincide with a big code change like rezoning, she said, because a big code change would require review of a lot of the code. Ms. Trombley said she was waiting for the big code change expected from the BPD Department to initiate the process. Originally the code change was anticipated in 2026, but it would be 2027, she said, so she carried forward the same figure for 2027. On the eCode 360 & General Code Updates line, also under Contractual, there had been a reduction. Ms. Trombley said it was hard to predict the accurate amount because the cost of updating the Town Code depends on how many laws pass, and how much impact each law has on the Town code. She gave the example that when a term is redefined, the change impacts the code everywhere the term appears in the code. Councilmember Stewart questioned if the Clerk could make her printers last longer. Ms. Trombley said they were being extra nice to the printers, since some of them are from the 1980s. She said the Supervisor had kindly offered his printer to Deputy Clerk 2 recently when the one on her desk stopped working. Supervisor Fish said it had been on his desk, and he didn’t even know what it was. Ms. Trombley said if one of the existing older printers breaks, they would look into modifying the front counter space to enable sharing between the two front counter workspaces. Reviewing B4020, Ms. Trombley said the cost for the Registrar depends on how many people die in the Town. The budgeted amount for the safety paper used to generate certified copies of vital records was the same as 2026. Revenue Councilmember Stewart asked if the Town Clerk thought any fees should be raised. She responded that rates for dog licensing had been raised in 2024, so she did not recommend changes. She said other Town Clerk revenues are mostly set by the overseeing agency, such as the NYS Gaming Commission for Bingo, and Town shares of Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) licenses, and the Town share of NYS Department of Health for marriage licenses. The 2% penalty for late payment of taxes is set by the State, and depends entirely on whether people pay their taxes on time and other fees collected in her office are revenues for other departments, such as BPD Department, and Recreation, she said. She said Deputy Jennings was interested in doing more to get dogs registered in the Town, and that she was thinking about doing some kind of promotion potentially in 2027 to raise awareness. GENERAL DISCUSSION It was said that Ms. Smith had presented a balanced budget, and with regard to potential surplus sales tax, she stated that she preferred to balance the budget and use surplus to address any deficit if one arises. There was mention that there would be no EFC payment due in 2027 as well, with regard to sewer financing. BUILDING, PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT (BPD) DEPARTMENT Ms. Smith said that she and BPD Coordinator Westfall collaborated to plan an increase in 2027 department fees by 3%. Mr. Westfall said he estimated a 10% increase in Building, Planning & Development revenue. Ms. Smith had proposed 12% increase. Mr. Westfall recommended sticking to 10%. Ms. Smith said this would take some off the sales tax figures. Councilmember Stewart asked if $10,115 goes to $60,000 interest. Mr. Westfall said it would carry over. Councilmember Stewart suggested $105,000 sales tax be allocated to the department. Ms. Smith suggested $140,000, and the Councilmember agreed. Reviewing account B3620, Mr. Westfall said he suggested a 4% increase for salaries. There was discussion about an increase for the Building Inspector and Code Enforcement/Building Inspector Peter Bachem, with Mr. Westfall suggesting $65,000. As with the Town Clerk, BPD Coordinator Westfall divided staff salaries across the 289 The Town Board of the Town of Moreau held a 2026 Budget Workshop at 7:00 p.m. on October 14, 2026 at the Moreau Municipal Building, 351 Reynolds Road, Moreau, Saratoga County, New York. budget lines that correspond to the portion of work done by each staff member. Mr. Westfall mentioned mismatched office equipment and furniture that he was budgeting to upgrade. Councilmember Killian inquired about monitors. Mr. Westfall mentioned 24” monitors to enable reviewing of documents. Mr. Westfall’s salary will be $91,208 according to the preliminary budget. There was discussion of the budget for the yet-to-be-filled Building Inspector role, with $63,000 for the new hire proposed. The figure floated as more realistic was up to $75,000. The figure negotiated for the budget was $72,500 with $24,000 to $25,000 charged to Enforcement, Contractual. Account B8020, Zoning—Mr. Westfall said it would be $75,000 for consultation leading to legislation as part of rezone phase 2. He estimated this could potentially be covered by fund balance plus a grant. Ms. Smith said fund balance being used one time for a one-time purchase was appropriate. Mr. Westfall said his department would need more BAS software licenses. Zoning Board of Appeals stipends under account B8101 and 2027 training for Zoning Board of Appeals and Planning Board members were discussed, with expenses allocated proportionally to the appropriate account. Councilmember Stewart asked why there was $50,000 under contractual. Mr. Westfall said it was because the big zoning update hasn’t taken place yet. Ms. Smith said it was possible to make a budget transfer to offset 2026 shortages. Next Mr. Westfall discussed more attorney reviews, training, attending the NYAOT annual meeting and conference, and memberships. There was mention of Mr. Bachem doing drainage inspections. A 4% increase for Mr. Westfall would bring his salary to $93,550, $65,000 was budgeted for Mr. Bachem, and $72,500 was set for the new Building Inspector. Bookkeeper Smith said overall retirement costs were increasing. MOREAU EMS Councilmember Stewart recused himself from this discussion. Bookkeeper Smith said Moreau EMS was getting the 4% increase they requested. Account A4540~-$407,540 was requested and included in the tentative budget. Reserve funds of $125,000 were added in 2026, and Mr. VanGuilder said that sum was included in this year’s figures again. He outlined the process of receiving engineering documents to submit to USDA, then bid packets can go to USDA, and then the squad can go to bid for the building project. He said no timeframe had been provided. Councilmember Donohue asked if the billing done by Moreau EMS is all income. Steven VanGuilder said it was, adding that billing and volunteer funds are kept separately. The Councilmember asked if there was a breakdown of what the Town is funding, mentioning that Moreau EMS payroll is over $1 million. Mr. VanGuilder said the Town’s funds provide 24-hour service 7 days a week unless there are already five calls underway. André Delvaux added updated equipment as a benefit to taxpayers. Councilmember Donohue said residents are billed by the squad if they receive services as well, so he asked what their tax dollars pay for. Mr. Delvaux explained that billing pays for services provided, and the Town contribution pays for ambulance supplies and the building. Ms. Smith asked how much of the $125,000 were reserve funds. Mr. VanGuilder said the $125,000 went into an expansion account, adding that the reserve is untouched, but also that it had not been put into a CD yet. Supervisor Fish asked when the mortgage payments on the new building start. Mr. VanGuilder said he did not know, that a construction loan was secured, and an additional $250,000 would reduce the mortgage. He said he was asking for the 2027 $125,000 reserve in their contract. He again said he did not have dates and offered to show receipts on the reserve account. The Supervisor said it was not a question of whether the squad had spent the money the Town had given them, but rather a question of how much the Town will pay before there is a building. Mr. VanGuilder was unable to say. Ms. Smith said leaving the funds in the Town’s account was gaining significant interest. Mr. VanGuilder offered to put funds into a CD. Ms. Smith inquired about a revenue stream 290 The Town Board of the Town of Moreau held a 2026 Budget Workshop at 7:00 p.m. on October 15, 2026 at the Moreau Municipal Building, 351 Reynolds Road, Moreau, Saratoga County, New York. PRESENT: John Donohue Councilmember Laura Garrant Councilmember Patrick Killian Councilmember Mark Stewart Councilmember Jesse A. Fish, Jr. Supervisor ALSO PRESENT: Krystal Smith Bookkeeper Erin Trombley Town Clerk Jeff McCabe Town Justice John Hogan Town Justice Chris Abrams Highway Superintendent Kristian Mechanick Water & Sewer Operator Reed Antis Town Historian Elizabeth Bennett Confidential Secretary OTHERS PRESENT: Maureen Dennis (Schermerhorn Real Estate Holdings) TOWN COURT Account Ai110F — Judge McCabe said there were $16.04 unused from the last JCAP grant which he was unable to close out, so they lost the opportunity to apply for the 2027 JCAP grant. He said the grant of $7,800 in 2026 paid for the new magnetometer, which he encouraged the Town Board to use during meetings. The Judge said records between 1957-1983 were completely digitized and with $20,000-25,000 more, all the court records to the present would be digitized. What remained in the basement archive, he said, was traffic ticket information, which has a 6-year retention schedule (unless the ticket was related to a DWI or criminal actions), and they are required to keep some records of a certain age as archival records, which they considered donating to a museum. He said the file room was now functional and not just full of clutter. The court had also removed all the court records that had been housed in the Annex building in 2026, according to Judge McCabe. He said they would get another $30,000 grant the next time around, and the loss of the grant for 2027 would not impact the court’s contractual budget. Account A1110 — Judge McCabe had asked for a 10% increase for the Court Clerks. Ms. Smith said Clerks had been given 4% across the board, bringing their salaries to 50,132, and an increase for hourly employees from $20.80/hr. to $21.63/hr., which is an $.83 raise per hour. Revenue — Ms. Smith said that in 2025 estimated revenue was $100,000, and the court brought in $162,000+. In 2024 she said it was just over $132,000, and the Justice agreed. She suggested they increase the figure for 2027 to $120,000, and Judge McCabe said they considered $130,000 or as much as $150,000. They agreed $130,000 was safe, and though the court had received as much as $150,000+ in the past, NY State changed policies so courts can no longer suspend or arrest someone who does not pay their tickets. If people do not pay, he said, the court keeps a running total of what they own and after a period of time, places liens, preventing them from buying a new car or house until they pay what they owe. He clarified that someone could get 15 days in jail or a $150 fine with $93 surcharge, and said if they sentence someone to jail they receive no revenue and the State frowns upon jail time for traffic and vehicle infractions. He said before the COVID-19 shut-down, revenue was at $145,000-$150,000 because if you failed to pay, your license would be suspended, and that is no longer the case. He said they were not supposed to be revenue-generating, but administering justice, and that was the justification for the change. Judge Hogan said that they let everyone know they can pay any amount they can afford—even $4 a week. Judge McCabe said NY State says a minimum payment should be $25, but they accept small payments because that’s 292

George Hoyt, Chair and Members of the Zoning Board of Appeals Village/Town of Mount Kisco 104 Main Street Mount Kisco, New York 10549 Re: CPD NY Energy Corp. - Application for Area Variances (Signs) 680 East Main Street, Mount Kisco, New York Dear Chair Hoyt and Members of the Board: Our firm represents CPD NY Energy Corp. (“Applicant”), the contract vendee of the property located at 680 East Main Street, Mount Kisco, New York (Section 80.72, Block 2, Lot 2) (the “Property”). The Property is located in the General Retail (GR) District and is currently improved with a gasoline service station and convenience store. On behalf of the Applicant, we respectfully submit the enclosed application for area variances in connection with the proposed improvements to the Property, including updating building and site signage (the “Project”). The proposed improvements reflect a reinvestment in a long-standing commercial facility and will enhance the site’s appearance and functionality. The renovated building, updated signage, and redesigned site elements will improve the visual character of the East Main Street corridor. Collectively, these improvements will modernize the Property, improve the customer experience, and support the continued operation of a longstanding neighborhood business. The Property has three road frontages – Main Street (NYS Route 117) to the south, Lexington Avenue to the east, and New Castle Drive to the west – which the Code deems a “twocorner lot.” (See Code § 110-59). The abutting commercial parcel to the north, as well as the properties at the Lexington Ave/Main St intersection, are all located in the GR District. The GR District limits freestanding/monument sign area to 30 square feet. (See Code §8910H(2)). This Project includes modification of the existing freestanding sign. The existing sign is comprised of two sign boxes on a single pole and has a total sign area of 45.37 square feet. The proposed sign consolidates the signage into a single sign box, and would have a total area of 42 square feet – reducing the sign area by 3.37 square feet and creating a more uniform sign design. Accordingly, an area variance for the additional 12 square feet is required. Phone: (914) 682-7800 Direct: (914) 220-9806 www.zarin-steinmetz.com 81 Main Street, Suite 415 White Plains, New York 10601 Village/Town of Mt. Kisco Zoning Board of Appeals CPD NY Energy Corp / 680 Main St October 27, 2025 | Page 2 The GR District also limits building signage to one (1) wall-mounted business sign. (See Code §89-10K(1)). The Project proposes to replace the existing building, which currently includes two signs on the front façade (facing East Main Street), including a Mobil logo sign and a Chestnut Market business name and logo sign. The side façade facing New Castle Drive also has a Mobil Service sign. This Project proposes to replace these building signs with Chestnut Market (name and logo signs) and to install a new sign on the façade facing Lexington Avenue (see below). Accordingly, an area variance for three (3) additional building signs is required. 4920-1635-7084, v. 1 Village/Town of Mt. Kisco Zoning Board of Appeals CPD NY Energy Corp / 680 Main St October 27, 2025 | Page 3 We request that this Application be placed on the Board’s November 17, 2026 meeting agenda for public hearing. In support of this request, enclosed please find the following materials: • • • • • Area Variance Application Form Environmental Assessment Form Building Inspector Denial Letter, dated October 27, 2026 Architectural Building/Signage Elevations and Floor Plans Survey For the reasons set forth below, we respectfully submit that the record establishes that variances to permit the proposed renovation of the existing convenience store. a. The Project Meets the Standard for an Area Variance Under the Mount Kisco Zoning Code and NY Village Law In determining whether to grant an area variance, the Board must weigh “the benefit to the applicant if the variance is granted” against “the detriment to the health, safety and welfare of the neighborhood or community by such grant.” N.Y. Village Law § 7-712-b(3)(b); Article VIII of the Village Code. This determination requires consideration of five factors, each addressed below. i. There will not be an undesirable change in the character of the neighborhood or a detriment to nearby properties created by the granting of the area variance. The Project will enhance both the Property and the surrounding area. The proposed signage is integrated into an updated building design that is more consistent with the character of the 4920-1635-7084, v. 1 Village/Town of Mt. Kisco Zoning Board of Appeals CPD NY Energy Corp / 680 Main St October 27, 2025 | Page 4 community, while creating a cohesive and uniform signage program. The Project also reduces the overall visual impact of the existing freestanding sign by replacing multiple sign panels with a single, unified sign box. In addition, the proposed building-mounted signage will improve wayfinding and visibility for customers approaching from different directions at the Lexington Avenue/Main Street intersection. Given the commercial nature of the surrounding area and the prevalence of multi-tenant commercial buildings, the proposed signage is compatible with existing development patterns and will not appear out of character with the neighborhood. Accordingly, the requested area variances will not produce any adverse impact on neighborhood character or nearby properties. ii. The benefit sought by the applicant cannot be achieved by some method, feasible for the applicant to pursue, other than an area variance. Second, the benefit sought by the Applicant cannot be achieved through any feasible alternative. The existing building signage is nonconforming. Even though the proposed freestanding sign increases Code conformity, a variance is still required. Further, the Project proposes only one (1) additional sign over the existing nonconforming condition. Given the location at an intersection and being located on a two-corner lot (having 3 road frontages), there is a need to have signs on the sides of the building facing roadways to enhance wayfinding and visibility to avoid unsafe driving practices. There is no other way to achieve this. Accordingly, the variance is therefore the practical means of achieving the Project’s functional and design benefits. iii. The requested area variance is not substantial. Third, the requested variance is not substantial when viewed in the context of the Site, the proposed development, and its impact on the surrounding area. 1 The proposed modifications to the freestanding sign will actually reduce the existing nonconforming condition by decreasing the overall sign area and replacing multiple sign panels with a single, cohesive sign box. The additional building-mounted signage is driven by the unique characteristics of the Property, which fronts on three public roads at a prominent two-corner intersection. As a result, the proposed signage is necessary to provide adequate visibility and wayfinding for patrons approaching from different directions. Moreover, the surrounding area is characterized by multi-tenant commercial properties with comparable signage. Viewed in this broader context, the requested relief is modest, appropriately tailored to the Site’s unique configuration, and consistent with the existing See, e.g., Wambold v. Southampton Zoning Bd. of Appeals, 140 A.D.3d 891, 893 (2d Dep’t 2016) (“While we agree with the petitioner that the proposed variance was substantial, there was no evidence that the granting of the variance would have an undesirable effect on the character of the neighborhood, adversely impact physical and environmental conditions, or otherwise result in a detriment to the health, safety, and welfare of the neighborhood or community.”); see also Lodge Hotel, Inc. v. Town of Erwin Zoning Bd. of Appeals, 21 Misc. 3d 1120(A), 873 N.Y.S.2d 512 (Sup. Ct. Steuben Cnty. 2007), aff’d, 43 A.D.3d 1447 (4th Dep’t 2007) (“Substantiality cannot be judged in the abstract; rather the totality of relevant circumstances must be evaluated in determining whether the variance sought is, in actuality, a substantial one.”), citing Aydelott v. Town of Bedford Zoning Bd. of Appeals, 6/2512003 N.Y.L.J. 21 (col. 4) (Sup. Ct. Westchester Cnty. 2003) (annulling zoning board’s denial of area variance application where “a review of the record reveals that the ZBA was, primarily, concerned with the extent of the deviation from the standards established by the zoning code without considering the impact on the surrounding community.”). 1 4920-1635-7084, v. 1 Village/Town of Mt. Kisco Zoning Board of Appeals CPD NY Energy Corp / 680 Main St October 27, 2025 | Page 5 development pattern in the neighborhood. Accordingly, the requested variances cannot reasonably be considered substantial. iv. The requested variance will not have an adverse effect or impact on the physical or environmental conditions in the neighborhood or district. Fourth, the requested variances will not result in any adverse physical or environmental impacts. The proposed signage will not affect access, visibility, light, air, drainage, traffic circulation, parking, or the physical conditions of neighboring properties. To the contrary, the Project will improve the existing condition by modernizing and consolidating signage, including reducing the nonconformity associated with the existing freestanding sign. With the exception of one additional building-mounted sign facing Lexington Avenue, the proposal primarily consists of replacing or modifying existing signage. As a result, the requested relief will enhance the appearance and functionality of the Property without creating any material physical or environmental impact. v. To the extent there is a self-created hardship, it shall not necessarily preclude the granting of the area variance. Finally, we respectfully submit that there is no self-created hardship here. The proposed work is intentional, but that factor is not dispositive. However, to the extent your Board finds that there is a self-created hardship, such a finding should not preclude the granting of the variance, especially if the Board finds that the other four factors weigh in favor of the Applicant. See N.Y. Village Law § 7-712-b(3)(b). Conclusion For these reasons, the Applicant respectfully requests that the Board place this application on its November 17, 2026 agenda and grant the requested area variances from Code Sections 8910H(2) and 89-10K(1). We look forward to meeting with your Board to review the Applicant’s area variance requests. Should the Board, its consultants, or Village staff have any questions regarding the application or require any additional information, please do not hesitate to contact our office. Thank you for your consideration. Respectfully, ZARIN & STEINMETZ LLP By: 4920-1635-7084, v. 1 Brian T. Sinsabaugh Village/Town of Mt.
