text: Westchester County Planning Board Referral Review Pursuant to Section 239 L, M and N of the General Municipal Law and Section 277.61 of the County Administrative Code Kenneth W. Jenkins Westchester County Executive August 11, 2026 Donna Atkinson, Planning Board Secretary Village/Town of Mount Kisco 104 Main Street Mount Kisco, NY 10549 County Planning Board Referral File MTK-26-002 – 118 North Bedford Road Site Plan Approval Dear Ms. Atkinson: The Westchester County Planning Board has received a site plan (revised June 23, 2026) and related materials for an application to expand the parking lot of an existing commercial building on a 2.79-acre site located at 118 North Bedford Road (SBL 69.74-2-1) and 126 Barker Street (SBL 69.66-3-15) within the OG – General Office district. The site is located at the southern end of the commercial corridor along North Bedford Road, with the Guard Hill townhouse complex and a single-family residential neighborhood located to the east. The North Bedford property currently hosts a three-story, 34,924 square-foot office building surrounded by a 121-space parking lot. The Barker property currently hosts a two-story office building, which is to be demolished. The applicant proposes to merge the two properties in order to reconfigure the existing North Bedford parking lot, and add a new 25-space parking lot on the Barker Street property, in order to provide a total of 167 parking spaces for the remaining building. The applicant is proposing to add this parking in order to allow space within the existing building to be converted into Medical Office uses, for which the Village requires a larger parking provision. 26,800 square feet of the building is proposed to become medical office, while 8,124 square feet is proposed to remain general office. The proposed Barker Street parking lot would be separated from the rest of the site by a series of retaining walls and landscaping, due to that portion of the site being located at a higher elevation than the rest of the property. Access would be provided from Barker Street. The existing North Bedford parking lot would continue to be accessed from two driveways, one from North Bedford Avenue which is northbound-only, and one from Barker Street. A staircase and sidewalk are proposed to connect the new parking lot to the existing building. ADA accessible spaces would be included adjacent to the building entrance. New landscaping is also proposed along the North Bedford Road frontage to increase screening for the existing parking lot. We have reviewed this application under the provisions of Section 239 L, M and N of the General Municipal Law and Section 277.61 of the County Administrative Code and we offer the following comments: 1. Site usage. While we understand that the Village/Town’s parking requirements for medical office usage necessitate an increase in the parking on the site, we question the need to demolish an existing, viable structure for 432 Michaelian Office Building 148 Martine Avenue White Plains, New York 10601 Telephone: (914) 995-4400 Website: westchestercountyny.gov Referral File No. MTK-26-002 – 118 North Bedford Road August 11, 2026 Page 2 the purpose of installing a parking lot that is disconnected from the majority of the site and requires extensive slope disturbance and a 14-foot retaining wall. We note that the provided documents indicate that a previous iteration of this application included a parking structure to accommodate the required increase in parking. This structure, however, was resisted by residents and removed from the plans. While it is unclear where this proposed structure would have been located, we believe that a parking structure located behind the North Bedford Road building, screened from the residential uses to the east by existing slopes and tree cover, would be preferable to expanding the impermeable surface coverage of the parking area and removing a usable building lot. 2. Transportation demand management. To further reduce the impacts of expansive surface parking area, the Village/Town and the Applicant should consider means in which to reduce the required parking on the site while tempering parking demand. Ensuring that the transportation needs of new uses are accommodated through means other than private automobiles is an important factor in reducing the dependency on cars and encouraging growth, without overburdening the street network and existing parking supply. The County’s Transportation Demand Management Toolkits provide strategies for municipalities, employers, and developers to reduce the need for single-occupancy vehicle commutes, which could help future visitors and employees avoid the need to park private vehicles. We recommend that the Village/Town and applicant review these Toolkits, which can be provided by the Planning Department, to ensure transportation needs are met while reducing the space set aside for vehicles. The County’s Smart Commute Program can also assist employers to implement TDM strategies. 3. Pedestrian access. We note that there is no dedicated pedestrian connection between the building and the sidewalks along North Bedford Road. We recommend that the applicant include pedestrian pathways to the building, separated from vehicular driveways and utilizing raised crosswalks, that would provide safe means for customers and employees to access the building from the adjacent residential and commercial uses, as well as the nearby Bee-Line bus stop. Transit access is a particularly important consideration for this site as medical office uses throughout Westchester have been seen to increase local transit usage. We also recommend that as the site is reconfigured, the Village/Town and the applicant should work to install a sidewalk along the Barker Street frontage of the property, in order to facilitate better pedestrian connections between the eastern residential neighborhood and the North Bedford Road commercial corridor. 4. Croton Watershed protection. The site is located in the Croton Watershed. Components of the site development may be subject to compliance with the New York City Department of Environmental Protection (NYC DEP) Rules and Regulations for the Protection from Contamination, Degradation and Pollution of the New York City Water Supply and its Sources. We note that a Stormwater Management Report has been included. Adequate erosion and sediment control and stormwater runoff water quality protection, both during and after construction, are of critical importance. Referral File No. MTK-26-002 – 118 North Bedford Road August 11, 2026 Page 3 5. NYS DOT review. North Bedford Road (NYS Route 117) is a State highway. The Village/Town should forward a copy of the application to NYS DOT to identify any required permits for the proposed project and to evaluate potential traffic impacts to North Bedford Road. We also suggest that the Village/Town work with NYSDOT to install a crosswalk across North Bedford Road at the intersection with Barker Street, in order to provide safe pedestrian accessibility to the site from the bus stops and points west. 6. Stormwater management. As the proposed site plan includes subsurface stormwater quality and retention infrastructure, we point out that subsurface methods of stormwater management can be of diminishing effectiveness over time if not properly cleaned and maintained. We are also concerned that the proposed underground retention basin would be located near an area of fill and a retaining wall. We note that a Stormwater Management Plan has been established. This management plan should include reference to potential impacts to the nearby fill area and retaining wall. The Village/Town should ensure the continued operability of this stormwater management system into the future to prevent the system from being clogged with sediment, and in turn force a higher amount of stormwater runoff into the Village/Town’s storm drain system. The applicant should also be encouraged to explore at-grade stormwater management solutions that treat runoff on-site wherever possible, such as using pervious paving for parking areas, or the installation of vegetative rain gardens. 7. Bicycles and personal e-mobility devices. We encourage the applicant to include a bicycle parking area for visitors and employees near the main entrance in order to provide full parking options within the site. We also recommend the applicant include a power supply for the charging of e-bicycles within this bicycle parking area. 8. Green building technology. We encourage the applicant to include as much green, or sustainable building technology as possible within the proposed development. The Village/Town and the applicant should give consideration towards the provision of electric vehicle parking capabilities within the parking lot. Should the renovations of the building commence in the future, we recommend that the applicant consider incorporating a solar array or a green roof in order to provide further environmental remediation within the site. 9. Universal Design. We encourage the Village/Town to consider the principles of universal design in this development, in addition to any building standards required by ADA regulations. Universal Design standards allow all employees and visitors to fully engage in our public and commercial spaces. Universal Design is also an important means of providing accessible pedestrian access and parking for persons with mobility issues. Referral File No. MTK-26-002 – 118 North Bedford Road August 11, 2026 Page 4 Please inform us of the Village/Town’s decision so that we can make it a part of the record. Thank you for calling this matter to our attention. Respectfully, WESTCHESTER COUNTY PLANNING BOARD Bernard Thombs Chair, Westchester County Planning Board BT/mv cc: Blanca Lopez, Commissioner, Westchester County Department of Planning Craig Lader, Director of Transportation Planning, Westchester County Department of Planning Millie Magraw, Water Quality Program Coordinator, Westchester County Department of Planning Heather Reiners, Smart Commute Program Coordinator, Westchester County DPW&T Anne Darelius, NYS Department of Transportation, Region 8 Christopher Lee, NYS Department of Transportation, Region 8 Nelsi Guzman, Bureau of Water Supply, SEQR Coordination Section, NYC DEP 34 South Broadway, Suite 300 White Plains, NY 10601 tel: 914.949.7336 www.akrf.com TRAFFIC REVIEW Village/Town of Mount Kisco TITLE OF REVIEW: 118 North Bedford Road & 126 Barker Street / Buckingham Properties Site Plan Application 118 North Bedford Road & 126 Barker Street (SBL: 69.74-2-4 & 69.66-3-15) DATE OF MEMO: November 6, 2026 ISSUED BY: Elaine Du, PE and Wyatt Gerber; AKRF This memorandum provides traffic comments on the 118 North Bedford Road & 126 Barker Street Site Plan Application. Previously addressed comments as of AKRF’s memorandum dated July 8, 2026 have been removed. Outstanding comments are presented in italic text, and new comments are presented in bold text. TRAFFIC COMMENTS PARKING UTILIZATION STUDY 1. 07/08/2026: The Applicant collected parking data on March 11, 2026 and March 12, 2026, which were mid-week weekdays while school was in session. It should be noted that the number of occupied spaces is approximately 45 to 55 percent higher on March 12 than March 11. Clarify whether there were any operational differences on the site that could explain the variation, and whether there could be even greater demand at the site. 11/06/2026: Comment addressed. The Applicant clarified that the variation in parking utilization was due to general variation in office occupancy. The parking utilization analysis remains conservative, as it uses the higher site parking demand to assess parking conditions. 2. 07/08/2026: It should be noted that the number of accessible parking spaces at the site should meet ADA requirements during construction. If any accessible spaces are closed for construction, other spaces should be temporarily converted to accommodate accessible parking. 11/06/2026: Comment addressed. The Applicant will maintain the required number of accessible parking spaces during construction. PARKING 3. 07/08/2026: The parking requirements on site plan sheet SP-1.2 are calculated based on 26,000 SF of medical office and 8,124 SF office, whereas sheet SP-1.1 indicates 30,000 SF of medical office and 5,024 SF office. Clarify the building program and update the parking requirement table as needed. 1 118 North Bedford Road & 126 Barker Street November 6, 2026 11/06/2026: Comment addressed. The site plan has been updated to reflect 26,800 SF of medical office and 8,224 SF of office. The site meets the parking requirement of 167 parking spaces per the Zoning Code. PEDESTRIAN ACCESS 4. 07/08/2026: At the proposed crosswalk which provides access to the proposed parking spaces at 126 Barker, the north side landing should have an ADA curb ramp. 11/06/2026: Comment addressed. 5. 07/08/2026: North Bedford Road currently does not have pedestrian access to the site. The Applicant should consider adding curb ramps and crosswalks at the driveway, as well as a sidewalk to connect North Bedford Road to the site. 11/06/2026: Comment partially addressed. The Applicant has revised the plan to include a sidewalk between the building entrance and the North Bedford Road driveway, including ADA curb ramps and an internal crosswalk. The Applicant should also consider providing crosswalks and ADA curb ramps at the North Bedford Road driveway. SITE PLAN AND CIRCULATION 6. 07/08/2026: Provide sight distance diagrams for the modified driveway at 126 Barker Street. 11/06/2026: Comment partially addressed. Sight distance diagrams were provided. However, the sight triangle to the right includes vegetation that appears to obstruct the required sight line. The Applicant should revise the plan to identify the necessary vegetation clearing on the south side of Barker Street. 7. 07/08/2026: Provide truck turning for a firetruck or ladder truck to show emergency accessibility to the site with the proposed curbing modifications. 11/06/2026: Comment partially addressed. The Applicant used a ladder truck with specifications comparable to the Mount Kisco Seagrave Marauder aerial ladder truck. The fire truck maneuvering plan indicates potential conflicts with several parking spaces or parked vehicles in the eastern portion of the site. The Applicant should modify curbing to provide adequate fire apparatus access. 8. 11/06/2026: The Applicant provided an Offsite Improvements Plan (drawing SP-1.4) showing traffic calming improvements along Barker Avenue. These include centerline audible roadway delineator, also known as a rumble strip, within the double yellow line between the painted island and Valley View Terrace; curve ahead and advisory speed signs; traffic signal ahead signs; and some clearing of vegetation along Barker Street. At speeds of 30 mph or less, vehicles traveling over the centerline audible delineator or rumble strip would result in a small increase in ambient traffic noise that would be slightly perceptible at adjacent homes. Within the vehicle, the rumble strip would produce a more noticeable increase in noise, providing an audible warning to the driver. The Offsite Improvements Plan should also be revised to include shoulder and edge line markings, providing a narrow shoulder where possible or painting the line on the edge or curb line where a narrow shoulder would not be advised. The Applicant should consider vegetation clearing on both sides of Barker Street to provide clear sight lines for drivers along Barker Street and for drivers exiting the site. 2 MEMORANDUM TO: Members of the Mount Kisco Planning Board CC: Donna Atkinson Lisa Cobb, Esq. Anthony Oliveri, P.E. William Seegmuller FROM: Jan K. Johannessen, RLA, AICP Village Planner DATE: November 10, 2026 RE: Buckingham Properties 118 North Bedford Road & 126 Barker Street Section 69.74, Block 2, Lot 1 Section 69.66, Block 3, Lot 15 PROJECT DESCRIPTION The subject property consists of two (2) developed parcels located at 118 North Bedford Road and 126 Barker Street; the parcels are located at the intersection of North Bedford Road and Barker Street within the OG Zoning District; they collectively consist of 2.79 acres of land. 118 North Bedford Road is developed with a three (3) story professional office building and associated parking and 126 Barker Street is developed with a two (2) story office building and associated parking. MOTION: ___ SECOND: ___ VOTE: Supervisor: ___ Councilman/Councilwoman: ___ Councilman/Councilwoman: ___ Councilman/Councilwoman: ___ Councilman/Councilwoman: ___ EMPLOYEE POLICY CELL PHONE AND PERSONAL ENTERTAINMENT DEVICE USE Purpose The purpose of this policy is to establish reasonable expectations for the use of personal cell phones, electronic devices, and entertainment equipment during working hours. The Town recognizes that employees may occasionally need to attend to personal matters; however, personal device use must not interfere with job responsibilities, productivity, public service, or workplace safety. 1. Personal Cell Phone Use • Employees are expected to limit personal cell phone use to scheduled breaks, meal periods, and other authorized nonworking time. • Excessive personal calls, texting, social media use, internet browsing, and other personal activities during working hours are prohibited. • Occasional, brief personal use to address an emergency or an important family matter is permitted, provided it does not interfere with assigned duties. • Employees should keep personal cell phones on silent or vibrate while working. • Employees must remain attentive and available to respond to supervisors, coworkers, and members of the public as required by their positions. 2. Entertainment Devices The use of personal entertainment devices during working hours is prohibited when such use interferes with job responsibilities or workplace safety. Examples include, but are not limited to: • Personal music players and portable radios. • Earbuds, headphones, and Bluetooth listening devices. • Streaming music, videos, television, or other entertainment. • Personal gaming devices. • Watching videos or accessing entertainment and social media platforms on cell phones or tablets. 3. Earbuds and Headphones Employees shall not wear earbuds, headphones, or similar listening devices while performing duties that require awareness of their surroundings, communication with coworkers or the public, or the operation of vehicles and equipment. Department Heads may authorize limited use in designated work areas when it does not create a safety concern or interfere with job performance. 4. Operation of Town Vehicles and Equipment The use of personal cell phones or entertainment devices while operating Town vehicles, machinery, or equipment is prohibited. Employees shall not text, browse the internet, watch videos, or otherwise interact with electronic devices while operating vehicles or equipment. If communication is necessary, employees must safely stop and park the vehicle or equipment before using a device, except when responding to an authorized emergency in accordance with applicable law and department procedures. 5. Town-Issued Devices Town-issued cell phones, tablets, and other electronic devices are provided primarily for conducting Town business. Reasonable incidental personal use may be permitted, subject to departmental rules and applicable Town policies. Employees shall not use Town-issued devices for excessive personal entertainment, inappropriate material, or activities that compromise Town information, security, or resources. 6. Department Head Responsibility Department Heads are responsible for communicating and enforcing this policy within their respective departments. They may establish additional restrictions based on the nature of the work performed, particularly where public safety, equipment operation, or public interaction is involved. 7. Enforcement Failure to comply with this policy may result in corrective action or disciplinary action, consistent with applicable Town policies, collective bargaining agreements, and employment laws. 8. Exceptions Exceptions may be authorized by the Department Head or Town Supervisor when circumstances warrant, provided that the exception does not compromise safety, service delivery, or employee responsibilities. CONTRACT AMENDMENT This Amendment to the Collective Bargaining Agreement by and between: The Town of North Elba (“Town”), and UFCW Local One (“Union”), representing certain Town employees. 1. Purpose This Amendment is entered into to revise the terms of the current Collective Bargaining Agreement (“CBA”) that governs the terms and conditions of employment of bargaining unit employees during the period January 1, 2025 through December 31, 2027 between the Town and the Union. 2. Term of Agreement This Amendment shall commence at 12:00 am on January 1, 2027, and remain in effect through 11:59 pm on December 31, 2027. 3. Article 30 of the CBA is amended to add a new Section 30.3 as follows: (a). CDL License Renewal Reimbursement The Town will reimburse employees for the expense of renewing their Commercial Driver’s License (CDL), provided that the CDL is required as a condition of the employee’s position with the Town. This benefit shall apply prospectively only and shall not be paid retroactively for any CDL renewal expenses incurred prior to the effective date of this policy. (b). CDL Training and Certification Expenses The Town will pay or reimburse the cost of the following CDL-related expenses for eligible employees: • One (1) CDL training course. • One (1) CDL road test. • One (1) CDL learner’s permit. • One (1) Drug Test (during training course). These expenses shall be paid by the Town or reimbursed to the employee upon submission of appropriate documentation and proof of payment, as applicable. (c). Reimbursement for CDL Training Upon Voluntary Termination Whenever an employee who has attended a CDL training course, the expense of which was paid by the Town, voluntarily terminates their employment with the Town within three (3) years of the last day that the employee attended the CDL training course, the employee shall reimburse the Town for the cost of the training course on a pro rata basis. The reimbursement amount shall be calculated as follows: 1. Divide the total cost of the CDL training course paid by the Town by 1,095 (the number of days in a three-year period). 2. Multiply that daily amount by the number of days remaining between the employee's date of termination and the date that is three (3) years following the employee's last day of CDL training. The resulting amount shall represent the employee's reimbursement obligation to the Town. Members of the bargaining unit specifically agree to such amount being withheld from their last paycheck as a deduction created for the benefit of the employee. 4. Article 29 of the CBA is amended by adding a new Section 29.3 to read as follows: 29.3 Random Drug Testing All members of the bargaining unit shall be subject to random drug testing as a condition of employment. Random drug testing shall be conducted in accordance with applicable federal and New York State laws and regulations, including Department of Transportation requirements where applicable, and this agreement. 5. Article 23.1 of the CBA is amended to add “Election Day” as an additional paid holiday (floating) to the list, thereby making thirteen (13) paid holidays. 6. Article 37 of the CBA is amended to provide that each wage amount set forth in the “1/1/27” column for wage rates for the respective job titles shall be increased by One Dollar ($1.00) per hour effective on January 1, 2027. 7. Governing Law This MOA shall be governed by the laws of New York State. 8. Signatures This MOA is agreed to and signed by the authorized representatives of the parties: The Town of North Elba: Signature: ___ Date: ___ Richard Preston, Supervisor, Town of North Elba_ UFCW Local One: Signature: ___ Date: ___ Joe LaPaglia, UFCW Representative___ Appendix 1 Town of North Elba Fund Balance Policy I. Fund Balance: It is the difference between the sum of all assets in a fund and the sum of all liabilities in the same fund. It is not comprised solely of cash balance. It represents the total accumulation of operating surpluses and deficits since the beginning of the funds’ existence. It is taxpayers’ money waiting to be used by the government for the benefit of the taxpayer. II. Purpose: For increased financial stability, the Town of North Elba (Town) desires to manage its financial resources by establishing a fund balance policy for the General Fund and all Special Revenue Funds that are legally mandated. This will ensure the Town maintains a prudent level of financial resources to protect against reducing service levels or raising taxes and fees because of temporary revenue shortfalls, unexpected one-time expenditures, emergencies, and disasters. III. Background: The Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) issued GASB Statement Number 54, Fund Balance Reporting and Governmental Fund Type Definitions. Statement 54 abandons the reserved and unreserved classifications of fund balance and replaces them with five new classifications for Governmental Funds: non-spendable, restricted, committed, assigned, and unassigned. The last three classifications comprise the unrestricted fund balance. The statement went into effect on June 30, 2011. The Office of the State Comptroller issued a bulletin regarding GASB 54 in November 2010 & April 2011 to explain the effects of reporting requirements on the Annual Update Document (AUD) filed by the Town on an annual basis. In addition, the bulletin references Chapter 528 of the Laws of 2000, which gives local governments the authority to carry over a “reasonable amount” of unappropriated unreserved fund balance. Due to the GASB 54 change in terminology, local governments are directed to apply the “reasonable amount” calculation to unrestricted fund balance. IV. Funds of North Elba: A. General (A000) B. Part Town General (B000) C. Community Tourism Enhancement Fund (CM01) D. Highway (DA00) E. Part Town Highway (DB00) F. Capital Projects (HXXX) G. Fire Protection Districts (SF01, SF02, SF03) H. Road District (RDXX) I. Park District (SP00) J. Consolidated Sewer (SS21) K. Water District (SWXX) (As of this policy draft, the only active Water District fund is Ray Brook (SW03)) V. Reasonable Amount: A. The unassigned fund balance for the General Fund shall not be less than 15% 25% and not more than 25% 40% of the total adopted budgeted expenditures of the Fund. A. The assigned, unrestricted fund balance of the Part Town Highway, Park District, and Ray Brook Water District funds shall not be less than 15% and not more than 25% of the total adopted budgeted expenditures of the Funds. B. The reasonable amount of the assigned, unrestricted fund balance of all other Special Revenue Funds shall be set annually when the subsequent years’ budget is adopted. C. Factors for consideration: 1. Composition of fund balance 2. Cash flow (timing of revenues and expenditures throughout the fiscal year) 3. Appropriations for the ensuing year’s budget 4. Established legal reserves 5. Dependence on the need to provide funds to capital projects 6. Prior year history 7. Funding of capital reserves, debt reserves, and other restricted assets VI. Classifications: A. Non-spendable (represented by account object codes 0806 & 0807) – Consists of the amounts that cannot be spent because they are in a non-spendable form. 1. Prepaid expenses 2. Inventory, only if the consumption accounting method is used. The Town does not use the consumption accounting method. B. Restricted (represented by account object codes 0814-0898) – Consists of amounts that are subject to externally enforceable legal purpose restrictions imposed by certain creditors, grantors, contributors, or laws and regulations of other governments; or through constitutional provisions or enabling legislation. 1. Capital Reserves 2. Tax Stabilization Reserves 3. Debt Reserves 4. Repair Reserves 5. Insurance Reserve 6. Other reserves allowed by State statutes C. Committed (unrestricted) (represented by account object code 0913) - Consists of amounts constrained to specific purposes by a government itself using its highest-level decision-making authority (Town Board). The Town Board must take formal action before the end of the fiscal year to add or remove a constraint. The use of this designation is not common. OSC believes that in most cases, local governments will not have committed fund balance to report primarily because reserves are allowed by State statutes. D. Assigned (unrestricted) (represented by account object code 0914 & 0915) – Consists of amounts that are subject to a purpose constraint that represents an intended use established by the government’s highest-level decision-making authority (Town Board), or by the Board’s designated body or official. The purpose of the assignment must be narrower than the purpose of the general fund. In funds other than the general fund, the assigned fund balance will be the residual amount of the fund balance. 2 OSC believes that formal actions by the governing boards (resolutions, ordinances, and local laws) constitute a constraint of resources and will result in an assignment of resources. 1. Encumbrances will typically be considered an assignment of fund balance. 2. Appropriation of Unassigned Fund Balance to reduce the tax levy. E. Unassigned (unrestricted) represented by account object code 0917) – Consists of all balances remaining after considering the other four categories for the General Fund. Use is least constrained in this category. In funds other than the General Fund, the unassigned classification should only be used to report a deficit balance. 1. All other unassigned fund balances in the General Fund. 2. In all funds other than the General Fund all residual fund balance, unless it is negative, must be classified as assigned fund balance. 3. In Special Revenue Funds, negative fund balances (excess of expenditures over revenues) must be designated as unassigned. VII. Policy: A. Reserves 1. Reserves are mechanisms for accumulating cash for future capital outlays and other allowable purposes. Unassigned fund balances are not considered reserves. 2. The Town shall strive to maintain a level of reserves to guard its citizens against a service 3. 4. 5. disruption because reserves are essential to dealing with unforeseen emergencies or changes in condition. Funding of reserves can come from surplus funds (excess of revenues over expenditures or one-time revenues) or other sources as designated by the Town Board. All establishment of reserves will be done by resolution of the Town Board (see Appendix 1). All expenditures from or uses of the reserve will require prior Board approval by the adoption of the Use of Reserve Resolution (see Appendix 2). Reserves shall only be used for the purpose for which they are intended. B. Fund Balance Policy and Procedures 1. The unassigned fund balance range for the General Fund shall be maintained within the defined reasonable amount. 2. The assigned fund balance range for Special Revenue Funds except for Fire Protection, Capital Projects, and Road Districts shall be maintained within the defined reasonable amount. 3. The Town Board shall review the assigned fund balance of CTEF, Fire Protection, Capital Projects, and Road Districts during the annual creation of the subsequent years’ budget and determine that all specific budgeted expenditures for such projects are also fully funded with budgeted revenues from grants, debt issuance, or operating transfers as necessary. C. The Budget Officer shall annually calculate and verify the Town Board’s compliance with this policy. In determining compliance, the following formula will be used: the balance available in the unassigned fund balance of the Town’s General Fund for the most recently audited fiscal year, divided by the adopted expenditure budget for the ensuing fiscal year for the Town’s General Fund. The same method shall be applied to the Part Town Highway, Park District, and Ray Brook Water District Special Revenue Funds using the assigned unrestricted fund balance. D. The Budget Officer shall report annually to the Town Board the results of the calculation and make recommendations for the use of funds in the event of a surplus or the replenishment of funds in the event of a deficit. 3 E. Surplus: If the unassigned fund balance of the Town’s general fund exceeds the maximum requirements, the excess may be utilized for any lawful purpose approved by the Town Board. To minimize the long-term effect of such use, the excess shall be appropriated to fund one-time expenditures, which do not result in recurring operating costs or other one-time costs including the establishment or increase in legitimate restrictions (reserves) of fund balance. F. Deficit: If the unassigned fund balance for the General Fund, or assigned fund balance for any Special Revenue Fund, falls below the minimum requirement set herein for any fiscal year, then the Budget Officer shall prepare and submit to the Town Board a plan to restore the balance to the minimum target level within an appropriate time frame, not to exceed three years. Such a plan when approved by the Town Board will result in the adoption of a Resolution confirming the action taken to replenish the fund balance. G. Application of Funds: In instances where expenditures are incurred that will require the funding sources to be comprised of two or more types of fund balance categories, the order of exhaustion of the fund will be as follows: 1. Restricted 2. Committed 3. Assigned 4. Unassigned VIII. Current active fund balance classifications for the Town of North Elba A. General Fund (A000) 1. Nonspendable - Prepaid expenses 2. Restricted for Repairs (offset with Cash Special Reserves account) - Fuel Dispensing System per Agreement for Fuel Services with Lake Placid Village & Lake Placid Central School District dated November 18, 2008. 3. Assigned, Appropriated a) The ensuing year’s budget b) Assigned for Encumbrances 4. Unassigned B. Part Town General Fund (B000) - The Town currently uses this fund for Mirror Lake Beach operations. The Village of Lake Placid pays 50% of the cost at the end of each season. 1. Nonspendable - Prepaid expenses 2. Assigned, Appropriated a) The ensuing year’s budget b) Assigned for Encumbrances 3. Assigned, Unappropriated C. Community Tourism Enhancement Fund (CM01) – The Town receives distributions from County Occupancy Tax passed through the Lake Placid-Essex County Visitors Bureau (also known as ROOST). These funds are set aside specifically for the enhancement of community tourism within the Town. (Tax Law §1202-s). D. Highway Fund (DA00) - Fund used for expenditures on bridges and major culverts. The proposed project includes the creation of a lease parcel with new utility services, parking design, drive thru lane, with an increase in green space. The property is now or formerly owned by Wegmans Food Markets, Inc. and zoned General Business (GB). Application #26P-0015, SBL # 139.02-1-2.3. 2. Cox Engineering, on behalf of Tyler Ocwieja, requests an informal discussion before the Board for a sketch proposal. The proposal includes a five (5) lot cluster subdivision on 5.60 acres at 1523 Jackson Road, Penfield, NY 14526. The proposed project includes the existing house and accessory structures to remain on one (1) lot with two (2) single-family attached dwelling units to be built with each unit on its own lot. The property is now or formerly owned by Tyler Ocwieja and zoned Rural Residential District (RR-1). Application #26P-0018, SBL # 109.02-1-18. The next Planning Board meeting will be held at 6:30 PM local time on December 10, 2026, in the Town Hall Auditorium to discuss tabled matters and other business that may be before it. text: Carmella Mantello Mayor Seamus Donnelly Deputy Mayor Christopher Marini Executive Secretary Peter Kehoe Chairman Planning Board 433 River St., Ste. 5001 Troy, New York 12180 NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING Notice is hereby given that the Planning Board of the City of Troy, New York, will conduct a public meeting at 6:00 P.M. on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to act upon the following requests for review and approval referred to by the Bureau of Code Enforcement. The City of Troy Planning Board will be conducting in-person meetings, however members of the public may attend and participate virtually by clicking the zoom link on the planning webpage. Members of the public are encouraged to submit comments prior to the meeting via email or in-person during the public comment period. All written public comment should be directed to planningboard@troyny.gov at least six (6) hours prior to the meeting. No other email address is monitored for public comment. Administrative Items 1) Adoption of Meeting Minutes of October 2026, by Resolution Old Business PLPB 2026 0064 – 75 Water Plant Road (70-7-7.3) [PC / CR] Site Plan Review – SEQRA (Unlisted) The applicant, NYS Marine Highway Transportation LLC, proposes to reuse an existing structure that was formerly used as a club membership, for a parts and supply warehousing facility. No exterior alterations or improvements are proposed. PLPB 2026 0078 – 207 Broadway (101.53-8-2) [DMU / DT I] Site Plan Review – SEQRA (Unlisted) The applicant, Cellco Partnership d/b/a Verizon Wireless, proposes the construction of an unmanned public utility/personal wireless service facility on a building in the DMU district. The proposal calls for the installation of antennas to be mounted at 3 out of 4 corners of the building near the top of the exterior wall, in addition to cellular and utility equipment located on an equipment platform on top of the roof. PLPB 2026 0077 – 110 eighth St (101.55-3-1./1) [CC/CI] Site Plan Review – SEQRA (unlisted) The applicant, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institution, is proposing to construct a new 15K sq ft child development center on an undeveloped portion of the RPI campus along Edgehill Terrace. The project includes 4 fenced outdoor playground areas, new sidewalks and a parking lot. Additional information regarding the above listed actions is available by contacting eric.ferraro@troyny.gov. As required by the Americans with Disabilities Act, auxiliary aids and services are available upon request. Please give one-week advance notice for services needed. Page 1 of 1

ADDITIONS TO THE AGENDA Town Board Agenda November 17, 2026 Page 4 BUDGET TRANSFERS - NO REPORTS FROM VARIOUS DEPARTMENTS REPORTS FROM STANDING & SPECIAL COMMITTEES SECOND HEARING OF CITIZENS ADJOURNMENT NEXT TOWN BOARD MEETING December 8, 2026 at 6:00 pm Town Hall Web Site address: www.townofcortlandtny.gov A Regular Meeting of the Town Board of the Town of Cortlandt was conducted on Octoberober 20, 2026 with the following elected officials and appointed staff in attendance: RICHARD H. BECKER JOYCE WHITE CRISTIN JACOBY ROBERT MAYES JAMES CREIGHTON Supervisor Councilmember Councilmember Councilmember Councilmember TOM WOOD MICHAEL CUNNINGHAM LAROUE ROSE SHATZKIN AMANDA SHAFIULLAH TINA TOBACK ANN SCAGLIONE MICHAEL PREZIOSI CLAUDIA VAHEY JOE BASSELL CHRIS GROSS Town Attorney- ABSENT Deputy Town Attorney Town Clerk Deputy Town Clerk Office Assistant Comptroller Director, DOTS Human Resources Coordinator Junior Network Specialist Director, DES Also present: MEETING CALLED TO ORDER The meeting was called to order at 7:01 P.M. PLEDGE TO THE FLAG Supervisor Becker started the meeting with the Pledge of Allegiance. SUPERVISOR’S PROCLAMATIONS & REPORTS Supevisor Becker commented about recent events the town hosted such as, a Festival of Maker with over 100 vendors, a Meet the Candidates event at the community center with congressional level, state level, county level, and local level, a Community Swap at the community center, The Road Nights Car Show with160 cars, Family Fun Day with Fireworks display, a First Responders golf outing, and a Senior Halloween Party. 1 Town Board Minutes October 20, 2026 Page 2 Supervisor Becker mentioned upcoming events such as, Town Hall Open House: Thursday, October 22, 5:00 PM where residents can meet all the department heads of Town Hall and learn more about what business is conducted in each department. The Unclaimed Funds Workshop hosted by Senator Peter Harckum run in conjunction with the Office of the New York State Comptroller, Thursday, October 22 at 1:00 PM at Town Hall. The Mobile Shredder is coming back to Town Hall on Friday, October 23, 10:00 AM–1:00 PM, you can bring your paper in boxes but no staples. National Prescription Drug Take Back & Car Seat Installation: Saturday, October 24, at the Purchasing Building. If residents have old prescriptions that need to safely dispose of them bring it to Town Hall. The Kids Halloween Hobgoblin Parade: Saturday, October 24, 1:00 PM at the Youth Center, ages 2–14, followed by the Annual Halloween Dog Parade: Saturday, October 24, 2:30 PM. Demystifying Medicare Workshop: Tuesday, October 27, pre-registration required. Anyone who's on Medicare or about to sign up for Medicare or about to retire, it's a very helpful program. The 250th Photography and Art Reception will be held on Thursday, October 29 at Town Hall, which will display patriotic photographs by adults and children, awards will be given to the best in class for both adults and kids. The Kids Halloween Party on October 31, 6:00–8:00 PM at the community center with tons of candy and games for the kids. The Veterans Day Ceremony on November 11, 11:00 AM at Muriel Morabito Community Center honoring all those who served and continue who serve our country. Please RSVP to the Supervisor’s office, the ceremony includes lunch and student essay reading. The Repair Café is back on Saturday, November 14, 10:00 AM–2:00 PM at Town Hall. The event allows resident to receive free repairs for lamps, appliances, clocks, jewelry, etc. Supervisor Becker and Councilperson Creighton along with the Town Board recognized Eagle Scout, Jackson Iriarte. He was honored for achieving the rank of Eagle Scout with Troop 238. His project rehabilitated the Hollow Brook Trail in Cortland Manor, including clearing/raking the trail, creating a landscape entrance, adding new trail markers, and building a bench. ROLL CALL Laroue Rose Shatzkin, Town Clerk took roll call, and all Town Board members were present. TOWN BOARD REPORTS Councilperson Cristin Jacoby gave her report OF NOTE: Councilperson Jacoby commented on School Bus Safety Week, reminding students to stay at least 10 feet away from the curb, until the bus comes to a complete stop and the driver signals before boarding, and remain alert while waiting. Motorists were also encouraged to drive cautiously, especially during morning and afternoon hours, stop when school bus lights are Town Board Minutes October 20, 2026 Page 3 flashing and stop signs are extended, and remain mindful of reduced daylight due to daylight saving time. She also introduced the town's new “Cortlandt Is Kind” initiative, a community program designed to support local residents in need. Launched at Family Fun Day, the initiative is currently collecting donations for the town's four local food pantries, with 100% of contributions going directly to the designated causes. Future fundraising efforts may support families facing hardships or other community needs. Residents can learn more and contribute through the Town of Cortlandt website. Supervisor Becker thanked Councilperson Jacoby on her leadership and work chairing the new IT Committee, which is focused on improving communication and integration between the town's various departmental systems. Working alongside Anne, the Comptroller, and Matt from IT, the committee is evaluating software and improving access to shared information across departments. Councilperson Joyce White gave her report OF NOTE: Councilwoman White recognized the professionalism, dedication, and hard work of town staff across Environmental Services, DOTS, and Purchasing, highlighting recent meetings with department directors to review quarterly updates, departmental needs, and priorities ahead of the upcoming budget process. Special appreciation was extended to Comptroller Anne for her financial leadership, clear communication, and guidance during challenging economic times. Councilperson White also highlighted upcoming resolutions supporting the Village of Croton's request for New York State DOT to address hazardous trees and prioritize repaving Route 129, emphasizing the importance of road safety. She also attended the New York-New Jersey Trail Conference Gala, celebrating volunteers and community leaders dedicated to preserving trails and natural spaces. Finally, she expressed enthusiasm for the restoration of the Briarcliff-Peekskill Trail bridge, recognizing the collaboration with Westchester County and local legislators and looking forward to a ribbon-cutting ceremony next year. Councilperson Robert Mayes gave his report OF NOTE: Councilperson Mayes encouraged residents to get out and enjoy the many town activities, and expressing appreciation to the Recreation and Parks staff for all their hard work in making these events possible. He also discussed the upcoming public hearing on proposed e-bike legislation, highlighting concerns about safety, particularly with Class 3 E-bikes, and asking residents to share their thoughts and help shape legislation that best protects the community. Parents were reminded to understand the rules and make sure their children are riding safely. Lastly, Councilperson Mayes spoke about the importance of giving back and getting involved in the community, whether through volunteering, helping a neighbor, or supporting a local cause. He encouraged everyone to find ways to make a difference and reminded residents that one of the simplest ways to have a voice in their community is to get out and vote on Election Day. Town Board Minutes October 20, 2026 Page 4 Supervisor Becker thanked Councilpersons Robert and Joyce for bringing attention to the deteriorating condition of the 50-year-old community center and for their work on the upcoming facility improvements. The Town has secured $850,000 in funding from the former Danish Home, designated to benefit local seniors, and plans to supplement it with bonding to renovate the building, including the bathrooms, flooring, exterior, and parking lot. Supervisor Becker emphasized how heavily the community center is used by residents of all ages and expressed appreciation to everyone involved in making these much-needed improvements happen. Councilperson James Creighton gave his report OF NOTE: Councilperson Creighton provided updates on several recent regional meetings and infrastructure projects, including an October 1st Hudson Valley Gateway Chamber of Commerce meeting featuring the New York State Bridge Authority's plans for rehabilitating the Bear Mountain Bridge. The project will focus on replacing the aging bridge deck, widening sidewalks, and installing suicide prevention barriers, while making every effort to keep traffic lanes and at least one pedestrian walkway open throughout construction. Councilperson Creighton also discussed the October 8th Westchester Municipal Officials Association meeting held in Cortlandt, where officials received updates on housing sustainability, local road conditions, and the need for increased state funding to maintain heavily traveled roads, including Route 129. Additionally, representatives from Holtec provided an update on the Indian Point decommissioning process, reassuring attendees that the facility will not be restarted and explaining the progress being made. Councilperson Creighton also highlighted several community activities, including Family Fun Day, the Hudson Valley Irish Fest, Hope in Hamilton, and the recent community swap, while thanking the many volunteers who help make these events successful. Congratulations were extended to the Cortland Community Rowing Association for representing the town at the Head of the Charles Regatta in Boston, with special recognition for its youth teams and cancer survivor rowing program. Upcoming events include the County Shredder at Town Hall on October 23rd and early voting ahead of Election Day on November 3rd, with residents encouraged to participate. Finally, Councilperson Creighton expressed appreciation for Councilwoman Jacoby's leadership in launching the "Cortlandt Is Kind" initiative, which will create an organized network of volunteers ready to support local food pantries, families experiencing emergencies, and other residents in need. APPROVAL OF THE MINUTES Approve the Minutes for the September 15, 2026 Regular Meeting. Town Board Minutes October 20, 2026 Page 5 Councilperson Mayes made a motion to approve the above Minutes, seconded by Councilperson Jacoby, with all voting AYE. PUBLIC HEARINGS 1. Public Hearing to consider creating Emergency Medical Services District #4. a. Close Public Hearing. RESOLUTION NO 230-26: Recognize Action as SEQRA Type II. RESOLUTION NO 231-26: Adopt Order. Supervisor Becker commented this Public Hearing concerns the consolidation of the town's various Emergency Medical Services (EMS) districts to help ensure consistent service levels and equal costs across districts. As a first step, the existing agreement needs to be amended to include portions of Croton within EMS District No. 4, specifically the Mount Airy Fire Protection District at the southern end of town. Councilmember Jacoby made a motion to Close the Public Hearing, adopt a Negative Declaration, and adopt the Resolutions, seconded by Councilmember Creighton with all voting AYE. 2. Public Hearing to consider an exemption for veterans with a permanent and total disability as a result of military service pursuant to RPTL Section 458-A (11). a. Open Public Hearing and Adjourn to November 17, 2026. Supervisor Becker commented this Public Hearing concerns proposed New York State legislation allowing veterans with permanent and total disabilities to receive a property tax reduction. The Town has postponed action until November 17th, 2026 to clarify whether the exemption applies to veterans injured in all wars, including Iraq, Afghanistan, and the Gulf War, and to better understand how the exemption would affect taxation within the Town's special districts. John DeBeneditics expressed support for the proposed property tax relief for veterans with permanent and total disabilities, noting that the legislation appears to cover veterans from multiple conflicts, including Vietnam, Korea, and the Gulf War. He emphasized that the 100% disability requirement limits the number of eligible veterans and that the financial impact on the Town would likely be minimal. He encouraged the Town to recognize the sacrifices and health challenges veterans face, including Agent Orange-related illnesses, cancers, and other serious conditions, and urged officials to support the tax relief without unnecessary delays or debate. Town Board Minutes October 20, 2026 Page 6 Councilmember Creighton made a motion to made a motion to adjourn this public hearing to November 17, 2026, seconded by Councilmember White with all voting AYE. HEARING OF CITIZENS – AGENDA ITEMS ONLY John DeBeneditics, raised concerns about speeding and traffic safety on Trolley Road, Watch Hill Road, and Lower Washington Street, referencing two letters received from residents requesting increased speed enforcement. They recalled a previous enforcement initiative on Watch Hill Road that resulted in approximately 220 speeding tickets and temporarily reduced speeding, but noted that drivers have gradually returned to unsafe speeds since the program ended. He emphasized the ongoing problem of reckless driving throughout the area and expressed the need for renewed speed enforcement to improve neighborhood safety. He also asked about the speed cameras and if they could be installed here in the Town. The Supervisor explained that the Town has strengthened traffic enforcement by hiring two fulltime county police officers, including a Community Resource Officer and a Traffic and Safety Officer, to patrol local roads. The Town also uses speed monitoring signs and increased police presence to discourage speeding, with officers actively issuing tickets, particularly during school drop-off and pick-up times and rush hour. Residents' requests for additional traffic measures, such as stop signs and speed bumps, are reviewed carefully, as these solutions can create inconveniences and maintenance challenges, especially during winter. For concerns involving road conditions or other safety improvements, the Department of Environmental Services evaluates the locations and makes recommendations. The Supervisor emphasized that the Town's approach is to prioritize enforcement and education while using the least disruptive methods to improve road safety. He also answered the speed cameras are not legal on Town roads. REPORTS Receive and File the following: For the month of July 2026 from the Recreation Department. W I T N E S S E T H: WHEREAS, the County has entered into a License Agreement with a private franchisee to operate and maintain bus passenger shelters at various locations within the County as well as provide advertising on bus shelters; and WHEREAS, the Cooperating Municipality is desirous of having the County provide bus passenger shelters within the Cooperating Municipality pursuant to said License Agreement for the comfort and benefit of its citizens. NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the terms and conditions herein contained, the parties agree as follows: FIRST: The County is hereby authorized to provide and maintain shelters pursuant to a License Agreement between the County and InSite Street Media, LLC, or its successors or assigns (the “County Licensee”), at locations within the Cooperating Municipality, all as shown in Attachment "A", which is attached hereto and made a part hereof. The Cooperating Municipality further certifies and guarantees that the sites designated in Attachment "A" are legally designated bus stop locations or that the sites will be so designated prior to the installation of new bus passenger shelters. If such designation is the responsibility of a governmental agency other than the Cooperating Municipality, the Cooperating Municipality will use its reasonable efforts to obtain such designation. Attachment "A" shall consist of: 1. A list of all bus shelters built under the County Bus Shelter Program located in the Cooperating Municipality. 2. A list of all necessary permits and the name of the municipal official who should be contacted. As the bus shelters are going to be provided as a municipal service, all permit fees shall be waived. In coordination with the Cooperating Municipality, the County may install additional bus passenger shelters other than those in Attachment “A”. Any new approved shelters will be installed according to site suitability and passenger usage. SECOND: The term of this Agreement shall be for five (5) years commencing retroactively on July 1, 2026 and expiring on June 30, 2031, which term coincides with the expiration of the License Agreement with the County Licensee (currently, InSite Street Media, LLC). A copy of the License Agreement is on file with the Westchester County Department of Public Works and Transportation ("WCDPWT") and may be examined by an authorized representative of the Cooperating Municipality upon reasonable notice to the County. This Agreement shall encompass presently existing bus passenger shelters and those constructed pursuant to the License Agreement. THIRD: Pursuant to the License Agreement, InSite shall pay for the cost of up to five (5) new bus passenger shelters per year, some of which may be located within the Cooperating Municipality. The design and installation of any bus passenger shelters to be erected within the Cooperating Municipality shall be similar to, but may vary in details from, the design drawings entitled "Westchester County Bus Shelter Detail" and dated December 2010, copies of which are on file with the Cooperating Municipality and the County (hereinafter, the "Design Drawings"). In no event, however, without the prior approval of the Cooperating Municipality, shall: (i) a new or replacement shelter fail to fit within the dimensions of its designated bus shelter pad, as set forth in the Design Drawings or, in the case of a replacement shelter, the dimensions applicable to that particular pad; or (ii) shall the size and illumination of the advertising signs vary from the illuminated advertising space customarily provided in existing shelters located within the Cooperating Municipality, as approved by the County and Cooperating Municipality, or as shown in the Design Drawings. The Cooperating Municipality acknowledges and agrees that the new bus passenger shelters shall be owned by the County. The Cooperating Municipality agrees to execute or cause to be executed any and all such documents as are necessary and appropriate to effectuate County ownership. FOURTH: The revenue received by the County from the County Licensee shall be divided between the County and the Cooperating Municipalities on a 50/50 ratio. The share of the revenue due the Cooperating Municipality will be determined by the ratio of that number of shelters operated by the County Licensee and producing revenue in the Cooperating Municipality to the total County-wide number of shelters operated under the License Agreement during one annual payment period. Payment will be made by the County to the Cooperating Municipality on or around August 15th of each year of this Agreement. Payment for August 2026 shall be due and payable within sixty (60) days after full execution of this Agreement. FIFTH: Pursuant to the aforementioned License Agreement, or other written agreement, the County represents that the County Licensee shall be required to hold harmless and defend the Cooperating Municipality and its employees, officers, and agents from all claims, suits, and actions arising from the construction and maintenance of the shelters. The County represents that during the term of the aforementioned License Agreement, the Cooperating Municipality shall be named as an additional insured under the insurance certificate provided by the County Licensee. SIXTH: All advertising to be displayed on the bus passenger shelters will be submitted to the County Commissioner of WCDPWT for approval. The Cooperating Municipality agrees that this approval shall be sufficient approval for the display of such advertising within the Cooperating Municipality. The County agrees that no political or religious advertising shall be allowed. The County further agrees that no advertising for tobacco products will be allowed, nor shall the County accept any advertising which does not meet reasonable standards of good taste. SEVENTH: The County shall use reasonable efforts to ensure that the County Licensee shall maintain all shelters in good condition. In accordance with the aforementioned License Agreement, the County Licensee shall clean each shelter on a regular basis, and shall be required to repair any damaged shelter. EIGHTH: In accordance with the License Agreement, the County Licensee shall provide snow and ice removal at bus shelters as follows: within forty-eight (48) hours of a shelter becoming reasonably accessible following a snow or ice storm, the County Licensee shall either commence removal or provide the County with written notice explaining the delay and the anticipated timeframe and plan for completion. Once underway, the County Licensee shall use its best efforts to promptly clear the shelter area and a path at least the width of the shelter to the curb, as well as adjacent sidewalks, crosswalks, and corner ramps, to ensure safe ingress and egress for pedestrians and passengers. Where ice cannot be safely removed due to hardness, the County Licensee may apply salt or another suitable de-icing material as conditions permit. The County Licensee shall work with the County to develop a coordinated snow and ice removal strategy tailored to each weather event, including communication protocols to ensure adequate preparation, and shall promptly coordinate with the County to prepare for, respond to, and support recovery from any State- or County-declared emergency. Compliance with these requirements is a material element of the License Agreement, and any failure to comply constitutes a material breach of the License Agreement NINTH: During the term of this Agreement, the Cooperating Municipality shall not enter into bus shelter advertising programs on its own. The Cooperating Municipality shall waive all municipal fees for the bus shelters. TENTH: If during the term of this Agreement any bus passenger shelter is required to be removed or relocated for any reason at the request of the Cooperating Municipality and upon approval of the County, said approved removal or relocation shall be done only by the County Licensee or the County and/or its contractors. ELEVENTH: This Agreement and its attachments constitute the entire Agreement between the parties with respect to the subject matter hereof and shall supersede all previous negotiations, commitments, and writings. It shall not be released, discharged, changed, or modified except by an instrument in writing signed by a duly authorized representative of each of the parties. TWELFTH: All notices of any nature referred to in this Agreement shall be in writing and either sent by registered or certified mail postage pre-paid, or delivered by hand or overnight courier, as set forth below or to such other addresses as the respective parties hereto may designate in writing. Notice shall be effective on the date of receipt. Notices shall be sent to the following: To the County: Commissioner Department of Public Works & Transportation County of Westchester Michaelian Office Building, Room 518 148 Martine Avenue White Plains, New York 10601 with a copy to: County Attorney Michaelian Office Building, Room 600 148 Martine Avenue White Plains, New York 10601 To the Municipality: Village of Mount Kisco 104 Main Street Mount Kisco, New York 10549 THIRTEENTH: This Agreement shall not be enforceable until signed by both parties and approved by the Office of the County Attorney. FOURTEENTH: This Agreement may be executed simultaneously in several counterparts, each of which shall be an original and all of which shall constitute but one and the same instrument. This Agreement shall be construed and enforced in accordance with the laws of the State of New York. FIFTEENTH: In the event of any conflict between the terms of this Agreement and those of its attachments, the terms of the Agreement shall control. [NO FURTHER TEXT ON THIS PAGE. George Hoyt, Chair and Members of the Zoning Board of Appeals Village/Town of Mount Kisco 104 Main Street Mount Kisco, New York 10549 Re: CPD NY Energy Corp. - Application for Area Variances (Signs) 680 East Main Street, Mount Kisco, New York Dear Chair Hoyt and Members of the Board: Our firm represents CPD NY Energy Corp. (“Applicant”), the contract vendee of the property located at 680 East Main Street, Mount Kisco, New York (Section 80.72, Block 2, Lot 2) (the “Property”). The Property is located in the General Retail (GR) District and is currently improved with a gasoline service station and convenience store. On behalf of the Applicant, we respectfully submit the enclosed application for area variances in connection with the proposed improvements to the Property, including updating building and site signage (the “Project”). The proposed improvements reflect a reinvestment in a long-standing commercial facility and will enhance the site’s appearance and functionality. The renovated building, updated signage, and redesigned site elements will improve the visual character of the East Main Street corridor. Collectively, these improvements will modernize the Property, improve the customer experience, and support the continued operation of a longstanding neighborhood business. The Property has three road frontages – Main Street (NYS Route 117) to the south, Lexington Avenue to the east, and New Castle Drive to the west – which the Code deems a “twocorner lot.” (See Code § 110-59). The abutting commercial parcel to the north, as well as the properties at the Lexington Ave/Main St intersection, are all located in the GR District. The GR District limits freestanding/monument sign area to 30 square feet. (See Code §8910H(2)). This Project includes modification of the existing freestanding sign. The existing sign is comprised of two sign boxes on a single pole and has a total sign area of 45.37 square feet. The proposed sign consolidates the signage into a single sign box, and would have a total area of 42 square feet – reducing the sign area by 3.37 square feet and creating a more uniform sign design. Accordingly, an area variance for the additional 12 square feet is required. Phone: (914) 682-7800 Direct: (914) 220-9806 www.zarin-steinmetz.com 81 Main Street, Suite 415 White Plains, New York 10601 Village/Town of Mt. Kisco Zoning Board of Appeals CPD NY Energy Corp / 680 Main St October 27, 2025 | Page 2 The GR District also limits building signage to one (1) wall-mounted business sign. (See Code §89-10K(1)). The Project proposes to replace the existing building, which currently includes two signs on the front façade (facing East Main Street), including a Mobil logo sign and a Chestnut Market business name and logo sign. The side façade facing New Castle Drive also has a Mobil Service sign. This Project proposes to replace these building signs with Chestnut Market (name and logo signs) and to install a new sign on the façade facing Lexington Avenue (see below). Accordingly, an area variance for three (3) additional building signs is required. 4920-1635-7084, v. 1 Village/Town of Mt. Kisco Zoning Board of Appeals CPD NY Energy Corp / 680 Main St October 27, 2025 | Page 3 We request that this Application be placed on the Board’s November 17, 2026 meeting agenda for public hearing. In support of this request, enclosed please find the following materials: • • • • • Area Variance Application Form Environmental Assessment Form Building Inspector Denial Letter, dated October 27, 2026 Architectural Building/Signage Elevations and Floor Plans Survey For the reasons set forth below, we respectfully submit that the record establishes that variances to permit the proposed renovation of the existing convenience store. a. The Project Meets the Standard for an Area Variance Under the Mount Kisco Zoning Code and NY Village Law In determining whether to grant an area variance, the Board must weigh “the benefit to the applicant if the variance is granted” against “the detriment to the health, safety and welfare of the neighborhood or community by such grant.” N.Y. Village Law § 7-712-b(3)(b); Article VIII of the Village Code. This determination requires consideration of five factors, each addressed below. i. There will not be an undesirable change in the character of the neighborhood or a detriment to nearby properties created by the granting of the area variance. The Project will enhance both the Property and the surrounding area. The proposed signage is integrated into an updated building design that is more consistent with the character of the 4920-1635-7084, v. 1 Village/Town of Mt. Kisco Zoning Board of Appeals CPD NY Energy Corp / 680 Main St October 27, 2025 | Page 4 community, while creating a cohesive and uniform signage program. The Project also reduces the overall visual impact of the existing freestanding sign by replacing multiple sign panels with a single, unified sign box. In addition, the proposed building-mounted signage will improve wayfinding and visibility for customers approaching from different directions at the Lexington Avenue/Main Street intersection. Given the commercial nature of the surrounding area and the prevalence of multi-tenant commercial buildings, the proposed signage is compatible with existing development patterns and will not appear out of character with the neighborhood. Accordingly, the requested area variances will not produce any adverse impact on neighborhood character or nearby properties. ii. The benefit sought by the applicant cannot be achieved by some method, feasible for the applicant to pursue, other than an area variance. Second, the benefit sought by the Applicant cannot be achieved through any feasible alternative. The existing building signage is nonconforming. Even though the proposed freestanding sign increases Code conformity, a variance is still required. Further, the Project proposes only one (1) additional sign over the existing nonconforming condition. Given the location at an intersection and being located on a two-corner lot (having 3 road frontages), there is a need to have signs on the sides of the building facing roadways to enhance wayfinding and visibility to avoid unsafe driving practices. There is no other way to achieve this. Accordingly, the variance is therefore the practical means of achieving the Project’s functional and design benefits. iii. The requested area variance is not substantial. Third, the requested variance is not substantial when viewed in the context of the Site, the proposed development, and its impact on the surrounding area. 1 The proposed modifications to the freestanding sign will actually reduce the existing nonconforming condition by decreasing the overall sign area and replacing multiple sign panels with a single, cohesive sign box. The additional building-mounted signage is driven by the unique characteristics of the Property, which fronts on three public roads at a prominent two-corner intersection. As a result, the proposed signage is necessary to provide adequate visibility and wayfinding for patrons approaching from different directions. Moreover, the surrounding area is characterized by multi-tenant commercial properties with comparable signage. Viewed in this broader context, the requested relief is modest, appropriately tailored to the Site’s unique configuration, and consistent with the existing See, e.g., Wambold v. Southampton Zoning Bd. of Appeals, 140 A.D.3d 891, 893 (2d Dep’t 2016) (“While we agree with the petitioner that the proposed variance was substantial, there was no evidence that the granting of the variance would have an undesirable effect on the character of the neighborhood, adversely impact physical and environmental conditions, or otherwise result in a detriment to the health, safety, and welfare of the neighborhood or community.”); see also Lodge Hotel, Inc. v. Town of Erwin Zoning Bd. of Appeals, 21 Misc. 3d 1120(A), 873 N.Y.S.2d 512 (Sup. Ct. Steuben Cnty. 2007), aff’d, 43 A.D.3d 1447 (4th Dep’t 2007) (“Substantiality cannot be judged in the abstract; rather the totality of relevant circumstances must be evaluated in determining whether the variance sought is, in actuality, a substantial one.”), citing Aydelott v. Town of Bedford Zoning Bd. of Appeals, 6/2512003 N.Y.L.J. 21 (col. 4) (Sup. Ct. Westchester Cnty. 2003) (annulling zoning board’s denial of area variance application where “a review of the record reveals that the ZBA was, primarily, concerned with the extent of the deviation from the standards established by the zoning code without considering the impact on the surrounding community.”). 1 4920-1635-7084, v. 1 Village/Town of Mt. Kisco Zoning Board of Appeals CPD NY Energy Corp / 680 Main St October 27, 2025 | Page 5 development pattern in the neighborhood. Accordingly, the requested variances cannot reasonably be considered substantial. iv. The requested variance will not have an adverse effect or impact on the physical or environmental conditions in the neighborhood or district. Fourth, the requested variances will not result in any adverse physical or environmental impacts. The proposed signage will not affect access, visibility, light, air, drainage, traffic circulation, parking, or the physical conditions of neighboring properties. To the contrary, the Project will improve the existing condition by modernizing and consolidating signage, including reducing the nonconformity associated with the existing freestanding sign. With the exception of one additional building-mounted sign facing Lexington Avenue, the proposal primarily consists of replacing or modifying existing signage. As a result, the requested relief will enhance the appearance and functionality of the Property without creating any material physical or environmental impact. v. To the extent there is a self-created hardship, it shall not necessarily preclude the granting of the area variance. Finally, we respectfully submit that there is no self-created hardship here. The proposed work is intentional, but that factor is not dispositive. However, to the extent your Board finds that there is a self-created hardship, such a finding should not preclude the granting of the variance, especially if the Board finds that the other four factors weigh in favor of the Applicant. See N.Y. Village Law § 7-712-b(3)(b). Conclusion For these reasons, the Applicant respectfully requests that the Board place this application on its November 17, 2026 agenda and grant the requested area variances from Code Sections 8910H(2) and 89-10K(1). We look forward to meeting with your Board to review the Applicant’s area variance requests. Should the Board, its consultants, or Village staff have any questions regarding the application or require any additional information, please do not hesitate to contact our office. Thank you for your consideration. Respectfully, ZARIN & STEINMETZ LLP By: 4920-1635-7084, v. 1 Brian T. Sinsabaugh Village/Town of Mt. text: TOWN OF RIVERHEAD PLANNING BOARD 4 WEST SECOND STREET, RIVERHEAD, NEW YORK 11901-2702 (631) 727-3200, EXT. 240 Edward Densieski, Chairperson John Hogan, Vice-Chair Ken Zilnicki, Member Joseph H. Baier, Member George Nunnaro, Member AGENDA Thursday, November 19, 2026 at 3:00 PM PUBLIC NOTICE TOWN OF RIVERHEAD PLANNING BOARD NOTICE is hereby given that the Thursday, November 19, 2026, 3:00 PM scheduled Planning Board meeting will be held at Riverhead Town Hall, 4 West Second Street, Riverhead, NY. All may listen to the meeting live by tuning into local channel 22. The meeting agenda will be posted online. The Planning Board may add or remove applications from the agenda upon its discretion, without further notice. The order in which applications appear on the agenda may be changed at the discretion by the Planning Board. Agendas may be viewed on the Town’s Website: http://www.townofriverheadny.gov. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE Zoom Information for Public Hearings ONLY Zoom information to follow. PUBLIC HEARINGS 1. Walmart Riverhead Expansion - Public Hearing on a site plan application seeking to construct a +/- 26,835 sq. ft. expansion to the existing Walmart store, located at 1890 Old Country Road, Riverhead, NY, within the Destination Retail Center (DRC) zoning use district, more particularly described as SCTM No. 600119-1-1.2 (Greg Bergman) DISCUSSION ITEMS 1. RD Pilesgrove LLC fka Reverend Vasilios Kapsalis — Major Subdivision — Discussion of a revised preliminary plat Cluster Plan for the Major Subdivision Application entitled RD Pilesgrove LLC formerly known as Reverend Vasilios Kapsalis, which was granted Final Conditional Approval by Planning Board Resolution No. 91 of 2008, dated October 2, 2008, in which the revised preliminary plat proposes the subdivision of a 35.8115 acre parcel into eleven (11) clustered residential lots, and one Agricultural Lot with a retained residential building area, with related site improvements, located within the Residential A-80 (RA80) Zoning Use District, situate 3544 Sound Avenue, Riverhead, more particularly identified as SCTM No. 600-17-3-3 (Matt Charters) 2. 534 Main Road Minor Subdivision - Discussion of a minor subdivision application seeking to subdivide an existing vacant, wooded, 3.84 acre parcel of 11/19/2026 Planning Board Agenda Page 2 of 3 land and create a four lot subdivision using Transfer of Development Rights (TDR's) to achieve the desired density, in accordance with Town Code. The property is located at 534 Main Road, Aquebogue, within the Hamlet Residential (HR) zoning use district, and is more particularly described as SCTM No. 600-662-13. (Greg Bergman) 3. 645 Grumman Blvd - Discussion of a site plan application seeking to re-use existing vacant industrial buildings as an indoor agricultural cultivation operation, perform site improvements including removing existing asphalt parking areas and revegetating with native vegetation, perform facade restorations, and perform an extension of the Riverhead Water District to connect to public water. Appilcant has received a Hardship Waiver from the Centra Pine Barrens Commission. Property is located at 645 Grumman Blvd, Calverton, within the Natural Resource Protection (NRP) zoning use district, an is more particularly described as SCTM No. 600-141-2-2.1 (Greg Bergman) 4. LCT Vineyards, LLC 2026 - Farm Stand Application - Discussion of a Farm Stand Application entitled "LCT Vineyards, LLC 2026" which proposes to utilize an existing 504 sq.ft. barn for electricity for an outdoor seasonal Farm Stand with parking areas located within the Agricultural Protection (APZ) Zoning Use District, situate at 1084 Union Avenue, Aquebogue, more particularly identified as SCTM No. 600-66.-4-1.41 (Marisa Danowski) PUBLIC COMMENTS ON RESOLUTIONS RESOLUTIONS 1. 2026-073 - LCT Vineyards, LLC 2026 - Farm Stand Approval - Resolution for a Farm Stand Application entitled "LCT Vineyards, LLC 2026" classifying SEQRA Action and granting final approval for a outdoor seasonal Farm Stand with parking areas located within the Agricultural Protection (APZ) Zoning Use District, situate at 1084 Union Avenue, Aquebogue, more particularly identified as SCTM No. 600-66.-4-1.41 (Marisa Danowski) 2. 2026-075 - RD Pilesgrove LLC fka Reverend Vasilios Kapsalis — Major Subdivision — Resolution to Classify an action as Unlisted Pursuant SEQRA and to initiate Coordinated Review amongst involved agencies for the Major Subdivision Application entitled RD Pilesgrove LLC formerly known as Reverend Vasilios Kapsalis, which proposes the subdivision of a 35.8115-acre parcel into eleven (11) clustered residential lots, and one (1) Agricultural Lot with a retained residential building area, with related site improvements, located within the Residential A-80 (RA80) Zoning Use District, situate at 3544 Sound Avenue, Riverhead, more particularly identified as SCTM No. 600-17-3-3 (Matt Charters) 3. Resolution No. 2026-076 — Town Square Hotel Project & Town Square Lot Line Modifications — Resolution Granting Two (2) 90-Day Extensions of Conditional Approval for the Lot Line Modification Application entitled Town Square Hotel & Town Square Lot Line Modifications, with said application made pursuant to and in connection with the Master Developer Agreement for the Town 11/19/2026 Planning Board Agenda Page 3 of 3 Square.
